description: This is a one-movement work that features lots of shifting characters and tonality often from major to minor or quickly tonicizing other key areas briefly. The opening section “Moderato” opens with a lyrical theme in the winds with interjections from the piano during their long notes or rests. After this statement a marcato espressivo section begins which combines double tongued sixteenth note passages in between statements of the theme in the winds with thick accompaniment figures in the piano. Eventually, a lyrical counter melody in the flute and other short motifs in the other winds are presented. This leads to a combination of all the short motifs occurring at once while the clarinet plays a more energetic solo. The next section “Lento” features a rhythmic dissonance by having half the ensemble in 6/8 playing a lilting quarter and eighth note melody while the other half simultaneously plays a passage of sixteenth notes leading to two eighth notes. Eventually, it becomes rhythmically consonant with the sixteenths becoming sextuplets. This returns to a reduced opening section which concludes with a virtuosic flourish of notes in rhythmic dissonance as the flute plays 14, the clarinet 11, and the piano 15 notes. The following section “Rapido” is a virtuosic piano solo with constant sixteenth notes. Eventually, the winds join in playing either sixteenth note passages or lyrical fragments. Next, a “Subito largo” section of three measures occurs in a chordal texture. The next section “Vivo” has an eighth note accompaniment in the piano underneath a leggiero melody of eighth and quarter notes first presented by the bassoon. This continues to be developed while other accompaniment and counter melody motifs are incorporated creating different contrapuntal textures throughout the section such as arpeggiated eighth note triplets and long notes with trills. Eventually the “Lento” section reappears leading into an “Andantino” section with rhythmic dissonance again consisting of scalar sixteenth note passages underneath a lilting triplet melody. Next, a “Vivace” section featuring a vocal-like melody in the horn overtop of weaving eighth note passages in the ensemble and a bass line in the left hand of the piano. Eventually, the winds come together playing the theme tutti overtop of thick accompaniment figures in the piano. This leads into a “Meno mosso” section with a similar theme in contrapuntal writing. The work ends with a “Calmo” section that is a chorale-like texture in the winds overtop of a triplet eighth note accompaniment in the piano.

description: This is a short three-movement suite in a neoromantic style with contemporary influence in terms of harmonic language and idioms in a similar style to Hindemith’s kleine kammermusik for wind quintet. The first movement “Marcia” has a quirky character in an ABAB form. The A section is a dotted eighth and sixteenth melody in the upper winds and an accompaniment that alternates between staccato quarter notes and a slurred quarter to an eighth note and eighth rest in the bassoon and horn. This leads into the B section that features a chromatic triplet sequential line that constantly drops and builds. The second movement “Andante” opens with a lyrical and legato horn solo consisting of eighth and quarter notes. Eventually, the oboe joins in with a countermelody before the rest of the ensemble enters with long tone chords. This leads into an oboe melody that has a quasi-improvisatory character. The next section features contrapuntal chromatic lines weaving around each other through the oboe, clarinet, bassoon, and horn. Finally, the movement ends with a flourishing sextuplet run in the flute and clarinet that sets ups the final “Piu mosso” triplet section comprised of a homorhythmic line in the flute, oboe, clarinet and bassoon that the horn responds to before returning to the earlier oboe melody. The final movement “Allegro non troppo” is a fiery character that features ascending triplets that constantly swell to sforzandos overtop of accompaniment figures such as quarter notes. The harmonic language in the piece often includes chromaticism and sometimes non-western scales such as the Ukrainian minor scale.

description: This is a short one-movement work in a lively character. It opens with a syncopated three staccato eighth note motif leading to a long note in the flute, followed by two in the bassoon, and then one leading to a beat of triplet eighth notes in the oboe. The second half of the phrase is a homorhythmic statement of an eighth note slurred to a long note. description: This is a short one-movement work in a humoresque character. The work is structured around two main sections with a form of ABCBA’A. The A section consists of mostly staccato eighth notes in an arpeggiated manner that are contrasted by slurred motifs such as dotted quarter slurred to an eighth note and eighth followed by two sixteenth notes all slurred together. The B section is lyrical featuring slurred one or two-measures motifs that are combined in a sequential manner to create a larger phrase. Rhythmically, it consists of quarter and half notes. A brief connecting section of a passage of sequential staccato eighth notes starting on a high “A” back down to the low “G” to set up a return of the A material. The brief C section is comprised of accented disjunct eighth notes. However, the final return of the A material has the material in a different order and some slight variations before a full original statement of the A material. The end of the A material undergoes a ritenuto that leads to a three-measure closing material of sixteenth notes leading to a long note to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work with a playful character exploring different major tonicizations and tonalities throughout. The first section features a dialogue between the ensemble. The horn and bassoon play a staccato eighth and slurred sixteenth note motif while the flute and oboe play a line of sixteenth notes that switches between slurred and staccato overtop of slurred quarter notes in the clarinet. Eventually, the ideas get combined such as the horn and bassoon motif overtop of the clarinet motif. This leads into the next section consisting of a lyrical melody in octaves in the flute and oboe overtop of chords in the rest of the ensemble. Later, the melody gets passed to the horn and bassoon with repeated quarter note chords in the rest of the ensemble. A return to the original texture occurs. This leads into the third section that takes the opening horn and bassoon motif combined with a march-like ostinato of repeated eighth and sixteenths in the upper winds. Eventually, the other opening motifs are reintroduced into the texture with variations such as the slurred quarter note motif now in a chordal texture in parallel motion. The work continues developing this material with the occasional introduction of new triplet eighth note material worked in to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work that shifts between a lyrical and sentimental character with a humoresque character. The opening section consists of arpeggiated sixteenth notes that lead to a long note. This is then contrasted with sequential staccato triplet eigth notes, which are interrupted by slurred and lyrical eigth notes leading to a long note. The opening material then returns. This is then contrasted with another humoresque section with new material based on two slurred descending eighth notes, sixteenth rest, staccato sixteenth in stepwise motion to a tenuto eighth note, sixteenth rest, followed by a final sixteenth note to start the motif again. It develops into a continual line of ascending arpeggiated sixteenth notes. It is then interrupted by descending triplet eighth note passage from earlier to set up another sequential passage of sixteenth notes. Afterwards, the opening material returns in a different tonal area. Some slight variations occur such as a trill on the long note for the third statement to increase intensity. One final time this is interrupted by a triplet passage that leads to one final trill and concluding motif to end the work.

description: This work consists of five short movements in contrasting characters with neoromantic stylistic tendencies structure utilizing elements of classical structure. Each of the movements does not have a descriptive title or character indication. The first movement marked quarter note equals 90 opens with short declamatory-like statements mainly comprised of triplets leading to longer note values that are in dialogue moving around the ensemble. Next, a melodic line in the flute consisting of arpeggiated sixteenth notes leading to a dotted quarter note that is followed by staccato eighth notes. This is overtop of accompaniment figures in the rest of the ensemble. The rest of the movement develops these motifs with brief moments of homorhythm or an echo-like texture. The next movement marked half note equals 60 has a chorale character, which gets more rhythmically active as it progresses and plays with dissonances throughout. The third movement marked quarter note equals 110 is built around an eighth note, sixteenth rest, and sixteenth note ostinato on a repeated note. Throughout the movement a triplet motif is in struggle for dominance creating rhythmic dissonance, with moments it prevails with the ostinato dropping out. However, at times it switches to dotted eighth and sixteenth note allowing the ostinato to be prevailing. The following movement marked quarter note equals presents a lyrical theme first in the flute that the oboe joins in on. As it progresses and develops the texture becomes more contrapuntal until there are four completely independent lines occurring simultaneously. This leads to a four repeated sixteenth note motif that gets passed around the ensemble to conclude the movement. The final movement marked quarter note equals 120 switches between various eighth note passages such as arpeggiated, repeated, and weaving motion. Eventually, a more melodic motif comprised of dotted quarter and dotted half notes is introduced into the texture. This leads to all of the passages being combined together to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work in a neoclassical style in a Rondo form of ABACA. The opening A section is a lively section marked quarter note equals 120 beginning in the lower register transversing to the tenor register and back down. It is comprised of syncopated motifs built around staccato eighth note and longer quarter notes with no articulation marking. This leads into short moments of four sixteenth notes. The B section is an Andante in a lyrical character that utilizes triplet eighth notes that weave in a quasi-arpeggiated motion. As it progresses grace notes are introduced to set up an accelerando that returns to A material. However, it is not a direct repetition of the A material but instead utilizing the rhythmic motifs with different harmonic implications. The C section is marked quarter note equals 70 also has a lyrical quality but features an eighth note followed by two sixteenth note motifs. The triplets in this section are now in scalar motion instead. It also utilizes the introduction of grace notes as the theme develops. This leads to the rhythmic motif from the A section that accelerando into the final A section. This time there are slight variations such as the eighth note motif becoming two sixteenth notes and the group of four sixteenth notes now being expanded to either six or eighth notes to elongate the phrase.

description: This is a five-movement work that Avidom turned to twelve tone procedures to imitate electronic effects displaying an interest in sound patterns. Often, part of the row will appear in a vertical manner rather than just horizontal. The first movement “Andante” features different contrapuntal lines that move one at a time composed of short motifs that continually loop. The second movement “Presto e scherzoso” is an inversion of the first movement that often omits the longer note values at the end of the motifs. The third movement “Adagio” is in a similar manner to the first movement but with different motifs. The fourth movement “Allegretto grazioso” is an inversion of the previous movement. The final movement “Andante sostenuto” is a recapitulation of the first movement.

Avidom’s music often can be characterized as a synthesis of stylistic elements of Jewish music and folklore, especially dance rhythms and East Asian music. This is a four-movement work combining these elements in a neoclassical style. The first movement “Allegro non troppo” is in ternary form that combines different energetic contrapuntal lines together in a march-like character that lead to brief passages of homorhythm for a couple measures. It features a rhythmic motif of dotted sixteenth rest (or tied) followed by thirty-second, dotted sixteenth and thirty-second. The B section “Meno mosso” occurs with the same motifs and similar material. The next movement “Allegro capriccioso” is also in ternary form and begins with a low drone on the pitch “D” in the horn with a dance-like theme in canon starting with the flute, then clarinet. The bassoon interrupts with a countermelody that becomes fragmented in the upper winds prompting a homorhythmic passage. The B section “Meno mosso” consists of a bass line in the bassoon and a syncopated eighth and sixteenth note accompaniment ostinato, and a scherzando theme in the oboe built around a dotted eighth and sixteenth rhythmic motif, large intervals, and brief flourishes of sixteenths or triplets. The return of the A section immediately combines the theme, drone and countermelody. It develops in a similar manner to earlier. The third movement “Andante sostenuto” features a legato and slurred theme built on large intervals and arpeggiations overtop of chordal accompaniment with various moments of counter melody inserted. As it develops the theme becomes more scalar in motion. The “Finale” movement has a ABABA. The A section “Allegro giocoso” features disjunct eighth notes in a two slurred, one tongued articulation. This gets passed around and built up as different instruments join in with various variations being combined in a contrapuntal texture. The B section “Moderato” features a rhythmic syncopated ostinato underneath an arpeggiated theme traversing up and down the range of the instrument in an arpeggiated manner of eighths and sixteenths leading to a longer note value. The return of the A material features different instrumentation of the parts. The return of the B section is greatly reduced. The next return of the A material immediately combines two voices together in contrary motion. This leads to a final homorhythmic scalar passage of eighths that becomes sixteenths from the bottom to the top of the instrument’s ranges resulting in a final Bb major chord missing the fifth of the chord to conclude the work.

description: This is a five-movement suite that explores five different characters utilizing elements such as form from neoclassical with language and idioms of avant-garde. The piece utilizes the full range of expressions that the bassoon is capable of producing from lyrical and cantabile playing to short and articulated. Movements one through three are based on Emily Dickinson quotes. The first movement “Love can do all but raise the Dead” creates a sense of longing and anticipation through an unsettled and wandering ostinato pattern in the piano underneath an espressivo and legato melody in the bassoon that avoids resolution by constantly extending the phrase. The second movement “Oh, honey of an hour” is a quasi-samba using a rhythmic and dance-like left hand ostinato combined with right hand syncopated figures in the piano. The bassoon plays technical passages often consisting of arpeggiated sequences or fragmented parts of scales combined together with rests creating an energetic and light character combined with atonal harmonic language to produce a quirky dance. The third movement “There is a solitude of space” creates a simple and melancholic character through an accompaniment piano and vocal-like melody in the bassoon. The movement takes inspiration from tintinnabuli, which is a compositional style by Arvo Pärt that is inspired by chant music by combining two voices of one arpeggiating the tonic triad with another diatonic mostly stepwise motion in a minimalist nature. The fourth movement “L’Allegro” is based on a quote by John Milton “Hence, loathed Melancholy… Mirth with thee, I mean to live.” The movement opens with a quarter and eighth note motif in the bassoon and piano that intensify and grow in flourishing passages of sixteenth notes. The final movement “Der Abschied” is dedicated to Valentin Bibik and is based on a quote by Taras Shevchenko “Proshchai, svite! Proshchai zemle.. (Farwell world! Farewell earth…).” The first section is a quarter note arpeggiated melody in the bassoon in dialogue with a quick articulated tremolo-like motif in the piano creating an ominous character. This leads the next section consisting of a more vocal-like bassoon line overtop of an accompaniment piano part featuring a sequential two sixteenth and an eighth note motif that becomes a simple eighth note accompaniment before joining in contrapuntal dialogue with the bassoon. This evolves into the next section that features a syncopated ostinato E in the left hand of the piano underneath dialogue between the right hand and the bassoon that intensifies through shorter note values and accented articulation. This section continues growing and variating while the ostinato changes pitches every so often eventually becoming an aleatoric section where the two hands of the piano slows down tempo independently from one another while the bassoon remains constant to end the piece.

description: This is a six-movement suite that explores the different colors the bassoon can achieve through many lyrical sections contrast with articulated playing. The first movement “Intrada: Stamping Dance” is a virtuosic bassoon cadenza that utilizes two voice part writing that evolve overtime into one voice before going attacca into the second movement “Scherzo I: Kozak Mamai.” The title references Ukrainian folk paintings of the seventeenth to twentieth centuries that portrays a Cossack hero often smoking a pipe while playing the bandura outside, usually with his horse nearby. These paintings have become a national symbol of Ukrainian culture. This movement is a fast scherzo featuring technical sixteenth passages and triplets with large articulated intervals overtop of a mostly accompaniment piano part with occasional moments of response and dialogue. The third movement “Aria: Tears” is a slow and pensive line in the lower range of the bassoon that grows into the tenor register overtop of a syncopated chordal accompaniment in the piano. The next movement “Scherzo II: West Wind” that features a sixteenth note motif in the piano that slowly changes overtime. The bassoon begins with a lyrical melody that later becomes sixteenth notes that join into a dialogue with the piano before returning back to the lyrical quality that dies away leaving the piano motif to finish alone. The fifth movement “Duma: Variations” uses prepared piano to imitate Ukrainian folk instruments. This is combined with a folk inspired melody in the bassoon that undergoes variations throughout the movement. The final movement “Tango” features a tango-like melody in the bassoon with a syncopated accompaniment in the piano that constantly gets interrupted by short virtuosic cadenza-like fragments.

The work begins with an ad libitum clarinet solo that presents the main theme in an improvisatory manner. This leads into a virtuosic cadenza-like arpeggiated passage in the flute overtop of a rolled piano chord. Next, an arpeggiated ostinato motif begins in the right hand of the piano, which the flute joins in on. The bassoon then enters with a legato secondary theme. Eventually, the flute develops into a virtuosic passage with a large glissando. This prompts the arrival of a contrapuntal texture based around short, fragmented motifs overtop of the ostinato still occurring in the piano. Eventually, the texture evolves to virtuosic ad libitum passages in an aleatoric texture. Different short fragments such as tremolos and quintuplet sixteenth notes are inserted into the texture to create a much more active quality to the music now. The music continues developing with different variations and new material being recombined until it climaxes to a dissonant frullato chord competing with an aleatoric piano line. A return to material from earlier in the work leading to a final chord that dies away to conclude the work.

description: This is the first movement “Slowly, sad” of a larger suite “Meridian” that combines a melodic line with rhythmic ostinatos to create an interwoven texture throughout. It has folk music inspiration but uses own original themes. The work begins with a melodic line based around the pitch “A” that expands outwards as it progresses. This overtop of longer note value chords in the rest of the winds that explore dissonance through open voicing. Eventually, fragments of the melodic line appear in the other instruments in a polyphonic texture. The next section “Lively” features a livelier variation of the theme in a contrapuntal and canon-like texture overtop of an oscillating sixteenth note ostinato. This ostinato gradually develops from a semitone motion to an arpeggiated figure as the section develops in some of the instruments allowing a more interwoven texture of four main parts occurring simultaneously1) main theme 2) fragmentation of the theme 3) semitone ostinato 4) arpeggiated ostinato, that imitate the flow-like state of a meridian. Eventually, a return to the opening material occurs that quickly adds in a fragmentation that rhythmic diminution from quarter triplets to sixteenth notes to create a final climax to a final fermata chord to conclude the work.

description: This is a three-movement double concerto for a violin and bassoon soloist that received the Lysenko Award in October 2017. Stylistically this work combines aesthetics, tonal, and extended techniques from avant-garde with allusions to baroque era, Mahler, and rock music. Artistic inspiration for the work comes from two epigraphs by poets T.S. Eliot “April is the cruellest month” and B. Pasternak “The selfsame blend of fire and eeriness prevails outside and in snug dwelling,” which are depicted through the dark and ominous characters and textures used throughout the concerto. The first movement “Allegro ma non molto” opens with an orchestral introduction based on staccato eighth notes that are a perfect fourth apart that slowly get more distorted with the introduction of quarter tones in certain voices creating an eerie atmosphere. The bassoon then enters with a main theme that has some rock music influence with syncopated rhythms and aggressive character through many accented notes and large slurred intervals overtop of rhythmically driven pizzicato accompaniment in the strings. The solo violinist then enters with a disjunct sixteenth note passage providing a disruption to the musical flow that was established. This leads to the violin taking over playing a more lyrical line overtop of the orchestral introduction, which the bassoon later joins in a dialogue with the violinist both playing fragments of the melody. However, the bassoon incorporates frullato to create a harsher texture. This develops into another syncopated and rhythmically driven section with motifs from the original bassoon theme, violin counter melody combined with more syncopated accompaniment figures in the orchestra. Eventually, the perfect fourth motif returns without any distortion in the orchestra. This leads to another lyrical section where the violin and bassoon are playing in an echo-like texture that finally unifies to conclude the movement. The next movement “Adagio ma non molto” opens with the perfect fourth motif that slowly gets distorted again but this time with three different rhythmic values creating a more contrapuntal texture. The bassoon enters with an ominous and vocal-like theme contrasted with a disjunct and aggressive pizzicato and striking the instrument passages in the solo violin creating two different characters attempting to coexist. Eventually, the roles reverse between the bassoon and violin. A final section that begins with fragmentation in dialogue between the soloists gets developed, becoming more active and virtuosic to climax to conclude the movement. The final movement “Presto ma non molto” begins with the bassoonist slap tonguing their bocal to create a popping effect while the solo violin plays pizzicato chords. This texture is interrupted by ad libitum glissandos in the orchestra. This leads into motifs and fragments of previous themes being combined together in orchestral accompaniment while the bassoon and solo violin are in a disjointed dialogue jumping around and pushing the maximum range of the bassoon. This includes jumps up to high F’s in the bassoon. This develops into an aleatoric section in the orchestra leading into a duo cadenza that features a string of sixteenth notes being passed back and forth over top of eighth note fragments that evolved into a full phrase. A return to the first movement orchestral introduction occurs while the solo violin scratches their strings and the bassoon plays multiphonics. Throughout this section a return to the earlier motifs such as major third rhythmically consisting of eighth note, quarter followed by a long note value that develops into the perfect fourth occur to conclude the concerto.

description: This is a one-movement work in a neoclassical style using typical forms, structures, and compositional techniques combined with aesthetics and extended techniques from the avant-garde movement such as frullato and glissando. The work opens with a “Moderato Sostenuto” section that begins with the flute playing the main theme alone in the middle register. As the theme develops the other instruments enter one at a time playing a drone, starting with the clarinet. This is taken over by the oboe, allowing the clarinet to present a triplet eighth note motif. This continues with the bassoon followed by the horn taking over the drone eventually leading into the triplet motif. The next section “Moderato meno mosso” is a homorhythmic texture composed of eighth and sixteenth notes in the oboe, clarinet, and bassoon. Eventually, the flute enters overtop of this texture with a virtuosic passage. Afterwards motifs from the opening of the section are traded around the ensemble. The following section “Agitato” features aggressive and articulated sixteenths notes in a texture of the flute solo in dialogue with the rest of the ensemble. This leads into a cut time section with a tutti syncopated ostinato leading into another homorhythmic section featuring tremolos. However, these tremolos are arpeggios that the musician quickly repeats similar to the effect aleatoric writing achieves in the avant-garde movement. Eventually, a clarinet solo emerges playing the main theme from the opening. This develops into a dialogue texture between the clarinet and the ensemble. Eventually, the clarinet drops out and this leads into a “Staccato sempre” section that features a bell-like line of long note values with a sforzando articulation in the horn overtop of staccato eighth and sixteenth fragments in homorhythm in the ensemble. Overtime the ensemble becomes contrapuntal. This leads into an espressivo and vocal-like melody in the flute and bassoon overtop of accompaniment figures in the oboe and clarinet. A return to an “Agitato” section occurs featuring a virtuosic quasi-cadenza solo first in the oboe that is followed by the bassoon and flute. This leads to a contrapuntal section feature motifs from earlier in the work. A return to the “Moderato” character occurs with a motif based off two eighth notes in an ascending third interval that alternates between minor and major is passed around the ensemble. A solo line emerges overtop of this texture that also passes around the ensemble. Eventually, this becomes an unison quarter note line in the ensemble with repeated triplets in the flute. This leads into a short quasi-cadenza moment in the flute interrupted by the staccato sixteenth motif from earlier. The work ends with a “Sostenuto” section that brings back the main theme in the flute overtop of drones passed between the bassoon and horn.

description: This is a one-movement work based around a theme with seven variations in a neoclassical style utilizing elements compositional techniques typical of a theme and variations. The theme marked “Singing calmly” is a five-measure vocal-like melody using step wise and arpeggiated motion that is presented solo by the clarinet. The first variation features the theme in canon with the bassoon starting the section with the clarinet entering two beats later. The next variation consists of the theme in the clarinet with a weaving counter melody in stepwise motion consisting rhythmically of eighth and sixteenth notes in the bassoon. The following variation changes key and switches the roles of the part with the bassoon playing the theme and the clarinet playing the counter melody. The fourth variation marked “Freely” divides the theme between the two instruments. The clarinet plays the first measure and then plays a whole note while the bassoon plays the second measure of the theme, which is marked “as an echo”. This same pattern occurs for measures three and four. For the fifth measure the clarinet plays the theme overtop of a dotted quarter in the bassoon that arrives together at a dotted quarter note with a fermata that fades away. The next variation features an eighth note arpeggiated ostinato bass line in the bassoon with the theme being turned into staccato eighth notes followed by an eighth rest. The following variation is polytonal with the bassoon in F major while the clarinet is in C major. The theme is rhythmically different and incorporates grace notes. The final variation is the longest variation within the piece and combines elements from earlier such as syncopation, grace notes, and counter melody motifs.

description: This is a five-movement work exploring many different textures and aesthetics of the avant-garde movement. Bibik was one of the first Ukrainian composers who turned to avant-garde musical language in the 1960s seeking to combine with traditional elements. Overall, his music is characterized by open emotionality, improvisation and spontaneity of development utilizing techniques of continuing variation of troping, massive canon, tone clusters, and simultaneous tempi. This creates a style that is based upon contrasts such as active sections with calmer contemplative sections. The first movement “Larghetto” is in ternary form. It features a vocal-like theme first in the oboe taken over by the bassoon then the horn in one tempo that is overtop of aleatoric weaving eighth note passages in another tempo in the flute and clarinet. A middle section with a duet between the horn with a melody and bassoon with an accompaniment. The return to A section has accompaniment long tones added to the texture. For the next movement “Comodo dolce” the whole ensemble is in the same tempo. It features an eighth note arpeggiated-like motif that is in a canon-like texture that gets developed into a larger line. This is overtop of long notes that turn into either frullato or multiphonics. The third movement “Allegro” is a quirky gigue like character with a theme of eighth and sixteenth note over larger intervals overtop of longer note values that incorporates glissandos and frullato to create unusual textures. There are moments of virtuosic repeated or scalar note passages throughout. Often, key clicks are used to contrast the louder sections to get a wide range of dynamic possibilities. The following movement “Larghetto” consists of two sections once again featuring multiple tempi simultaneously occurring. The first has a melodic line overtop of accompaniment texture, often half notes and occasional moments of echoing the solo line. The second is homorhythmic section in a cluster chord harmony. The final movement “Larghetto” has two main sections. The first section has the same material as the A section in the first movement but different instrumentation. The theme is in the flute with aleatoric material in the clarinet and bassoon and the B theme in the horn. There is new material added in the oboe as interjections. The second section consists of air noises using graphic notation leading to a final tutti multiphonic to conclude the piece.

description: This is a short one-movement work based around a Psalm sung in Ukrainian by a soprano with accompaniment figures in the ensemble. The piano opens with a motif of constant eighth notes that shift around chromatic harmonies. When the vocalist enters, the piano plays cluster chords on the downbeat with pizzicato chords in the strings. Eventually, the piano returns to their original motif with a countermelody in the strings underneath the vocalist. This leads into a section where the bassoon and tuba play air noise notes, and the strings play notes without sound like wind underneath the vocalist. description: This is a short one-movement work that explores rhythmic ostinatos that are in rhythmic dissonance in constantly shifting meters. The piano provides a continual texture of constant sextuplet sixteenth notes in an arpeggiated motion in the right hand against thirty-second notes in ascending chromatic motion. The tuba provides grounding points by playing a quarter note followed by rests only in the 3/4 measures. However, the quarter note alternates between being on beat 1 and 3. The bassoon has a line of staccato eighth notes in large intervals, which always begins on the offbeat. The work ends with the piano playing their ostinato alone dying away to pianississimo.

description: This work consists of three miniatures with no titles given but is differentiated by metronome marking. The first miniature “quarter note equals 70” features a legato and sorrowful melody that develops and grows over lush harmonies. Through this development a variety of different accompaniment textures such as chordal and contrapuntal are explored to change the character. The second miniature “quarter note equals 85” is a humoresque and ironic waltz. The movement opens with a disjointed trading notes texture amongst the ensemble leading to a waltz-like accompaniment in the bassoons that stumbles onto a dissonant semitone fermata chord twice before being able to successfully continue. The violin then joins in with a sneaky melody that weaves around. Eventually, the first bassoon takes over with a second melody overtop of an arpeggiated accompaniment in the second bassoon. The violin then rejoins with a countermelody before returning to the material similar to the original motifs before arriving at an aggressive and accented coda. The third miniature “quarter note equals 220” has an energetic character through the articulated motifs combined with a constant rhythmic pulse of alternating eighth note and quarter notes that is constantly being thrown off due to the alternating pattern of accents and changing meter.

description: This is a three-movement suite that combines elements of folk music such as melody, rhythm, and harmony. This work was written prior to his immigration to Finland. The first movement “The Endless Wintry Steppe” opens with an “Andante” section that consists of a vocal-like melody that gets passed around the ensemble overtop of chords. This is starkly contrasted with an “Allegro” section that has ominous eighth note chords followed by an eighth rest in the ensemble underneath weaving triplet eighth notes in the flute. As it develops it becomes sixteenth notes in the flute and more lyrical lines are presented in the ensemble consisting of eighth, quarter, and half notes. A two measure return of the opening material occurs with a caesura that is followed by an open fifth whole note chord of the pitches “Bb” and “F” in the ensemble. The following movement “Spring Flow” is in an allegro tempo with an energetic dance-like character. It features a playful theme first presented by the flute that gets fragmented and passed around the ensemble. This is overtop of offbeat staccato eighth notes and half note trills. The final movement “Morning on the Steppe” has a pastorale character with a semplice theme of quarter followed by either an eighth or two sixteenth notes leading to a trill dotted quarter note that is first presented by the flute. This is overtop of dotted quarter note chords and a countermelody comprised of eighth notes with two sixteenth grace notes in the middle. The movement continues developing these motifs until arriving back at the original material to conclude the work.

description: Bruk’s style once immigrating to Finland has been described as “embracing native Finnish material in a way that nourishes his own distinctive brand of early twentieth-century free-tonal music.”16 The work is a five-movement suite that goes through a variety of styles and characters. The first movement “Mirage” opens with a cantus-firmus like line that gradually becomes more active and intricate as it develops going through various forms and textures such as trading eighth notes and trilled quarter notes. The next movement “The Old Dance” is in ternary form and features an eighth note waltz-like bass line in the bassoon that develops in sixteenth notes. Throughout the movement it alternates between the eighth and various sixteenth note variations. The theme is mostly a virtuosic display of sixteenth notes. The “Meno mosso” features a theme composed of quarter and eighth notes in the clarinet overtop of a bass line that combines arpeggiated and scalar motion in the bassoon. The following movement “Invention à la Shostakovich” is centered around a rhythmic motif of a dotted eighth followed by a sixteenth (and its reverse) that briefly becomes three triplet eighth notes. It is mainly in a dialogue texture. The fourth movement “March à la Prokofiev” has triplet and dotted eighth followed by sixteenth motifs that pass back and forth that develop into brief homorhythmic statements. The final movement “The Autumnal Shadows” consists of a lyrical and vocal-like theme in the clarinet and three arpeggiated staccato eighth note accompaniment in the bassoon. Halfway through the roles switch with the clarinet now playing five eighth notes starting on the second eighth of the bar while the bassoon plays a waltz-like theme. Eventually, the two instruments play the accompaniment line together in harmony. The work concludes with the bassoon returning to the theme with a fragmented accompaniment from the clarinet.

description: This is a two-movement work in a neoclassical style that occasionally explores some avant-garde techniques such as frullato and unconventional notations. The first movement “Acuto” consists of two contrapuntal lines that lead to brief solo moments. The lines often contain technical passages of sixteenth notes that are contrasted with a dotted eighth and sixteenth note motif. As it develops the motifs combined into one line. There are some homorhythmic passages that explore texture by the use of contemporary techniques such as frullato in the bassoon while the horn plays ordinarily. The second movement “Variations on an Own Theme” consists of a theme in the horn built mainly on eighth and quarter notes with the occasional sixteenth notes leading to the next beat with a contrapuntal line in the bassoon. The first variation slightly varied in both the theme and the accompaniment. The second variation has a dance-like character shifting it into a triple metre. The third variation rhythmically augments the theme at times and changes aspects to a dotted eighth followed by a sixteenth motif. The accompaniment to an arpeggiated line in various rhythms. The fourth variation puts the theme in a dotted eighth followed by a sixteenth motif. The fifth variation has a waltz-like character in a triple metre. The accompaniment is often syncopated. The final variation begins with the instruments creating a constant line of staccato sixteenth notes. Then a “meno mosso” section creates a cantabile version of the theme before returning to the sixteenth note texture.

description: This is a short one-movement work based on Ukrainian folk songs that undergo a variety of contrasting sections from lyrical, humoresque, and virtuosic. The opening section “Moderato piu mosso Agitato” that reoccurs throughout the piece. It consists of an energetic theme in the bassoon of staccato eight and sixteenth notes with the occasional mordent. This is overtop of accompaniment chords on the beats in the strings. The next section “Adagio Lento piu mosso features a lyrical and vocal-like theme in the bassoon in a molto legato manner mainly in step-wise of intervals of a perfect fourth and fifth overtop of a rhythmic ostinato of half note followed by a quarter note providing harmonic support. The following section “Moderato piu mosso” features another new theme in a lyrical style based around of dotted eight and sixteenth followed by two eighth notes overtop of a bass line in the lower strings and an oscillating perfect fifth ostinato in the upper strings. As it develops rhythmic diminution occurs from eight to sixteenths in the upper strings and quarter to eight in the lower strings to create more intensity. An orchestral interlude occurs where the violins take over the melody. A two-measure bassoon cadenza sets up the key change to the same name minor that combines elements from earlier in the section with material from the beginning A section. The following section “Andante” has a lyrical and vocal-like melody comprised of half, quarter, dotted quarter followed by an eighth note rhythm. The strings play accompaniment motifs underneath such as whole notes and oscillating eighth note patterns. Finally, the opening A section returns in a full restatement. This leads into a section that is a synthesize of earlier material ending with an orchestral interlude that sets up an extended bassoon cadenza in a virtuosic manner that traverses throughout the range of the bassoon in an arpeggiated and sequential manner. A final virtuosic section occurs featuring extended passages of sixteenth notes in the bassoon while the strings bring back themes and motifs from earlier underneath leading to one final statement of a variation on the A material to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work based on outer space. The Corona Australis is a constellation in the southern hemisphere of the sky discovered by the Greek astronomer Claudius Ptolemy in the second century. Musically, the piece explores timbre and rhythm by flowing between slight changes occurring over time. The piece has an unusual form that has a couple main motifs and sections that return and are transformed. The piece begins with an A section consisting of multiphonic whole notes in a staggered entry not in any pattern. Then a B section comprised of dotted quarter note where different instruments drop out at random intervals revealing a wide variety of textures, colors and timbres available in a woodwind quartet through exploring as many possible instrumental combinations. Then the main motivic material is introduced in the C section which is a syncopated sixteenth note melody that develops into a thirty-second note motif in the flute over top of an accompaniment ostinato that alternates between consonance and dissonance. Then a two-measure interruption involving the bassoon knocking on the body of the instrument leading to a repetition of the thirty-second note motif beginning with the bassoon, and staggered entry by the oboe and flute overtop of a syncopated repeated note ostinato in the clarinet. Then a one-measure unison 5:4 eighth note motif is played by the entire ensemble to lead back to the A section. This then leads to a staggered entry of the syncopated clarinet motif but this time it is on the beat that develops in intensity through quicker rhythm and louder dynamics until the thirty-second motif of the C section returns. Then the B section comes back but instead starts on beat four instead of the downbeat. This grows dynamically until arriving at forte which simultaneously becomes the four measure Coda consisting of rhythmically unison chords.

description: This is a one-movement work inspired by outer space. Naiad is a satellite of Neptune with an irregular and nonspherical shape that was discovered by the Voyager-2 spacecraft in 1989. The word Naiad originates from mythology, which are female spirits or nymphs that gather around springs, streams and brooks. Overall, the composition is based upon free atonality with elements of serial music and micro-series. It utilizes cluster consonances from the series and micro-series throughout the piece to harmonically tie the work together. Polyrhythms are used to create different rhythmic frameworks within the piece. The work explores different register contrasts and timbral contrasts through his own symbols and unconventional directions to achieve a new quality of sound for the listener’s perceptual analysis of the score. The form of the piece is Intro, ABCBDBA, Coda. The piece opens with a short introduction of the piano plucking the strings. This leads into the A section of aggressive long notes in the bassoon in unison with cluster chords in the piano. This leads to the B section which consists of multiphonic notes that utilize goat-vibrato (vibrato produced with the lips like a saxophonist) and pitch bending over top of a 7:4 quarter note motif in the piano. This develops by the bassoon joining into the motif on the eighth note level and eventually progressing to the sixteenth note level. This leads to the C section consisting of a passage that is a string of thirty-second note that the bassoonist and piano weave around one another. The piece then goes back to the B section. Then a new D section is presented using elements of aleatorism and improvising. Then the piece returns to the B section, except the second motif is presented first this time. Then the A section returns leading into a coda that incorporates the string plucking from the introduction with the bassoon playing whole notes in the low register.

This develops and then fades away into glissandos in the flute and piano that the bassoon responds with a quasi-cadenza featuring the use of a multiphonic. The flute takes over with a passage of harmonics with short interjections from the bassoon and piano to conclude the piece.

description: This is a short one-movement work in three main sections based on popular Italian songs of the 1930s and 1960s. The work is based on the principle of citation from the postmodernist movement characterized by its inherent stylistic beats, the play of images, contrasts, and re-interpretation of meanings throughout. The opening “Tempo improvizato” is structured as a one measure piano introduction that leads into a homorhythmic flute and bassoon melody. The piano responds with fragments to this melody during their longer note values. As the piece progresses the flute and bassoon begin to deviate into a more contrapuntal texture, while the piano becomes more active with larger phrases until it becomes a full accompaniment. The next section “Molto piu mosso” continues this accompaniment texture in the piano with the flute and bassoon returning to a homorhythmic line that turns into a call and response. The final section “Lento” consists of two independent lines in the flute and bassoon overtop of a simple eighth note accompaniment in the piano that slows down into chords, which the flute and bassoon trill dotted half notes over top of to conclude the piece.

description: This is a five-movement work that combines elements of postmodernism and neoimpressionism to explore a wide variety of characters and textures in quintet playing. The first movement “Shlyakh kohannya” (Via d’amore) is in a slower tempo with the direction “Langrilur ma nobile” that opens with a homorhythmic line in a descending motion in the flute, oboe, and clarinet that the horn and bassoon respond with accented long notes. This texture develops in a quasi-cadenza moment in the flute that the oboe joins midway. This leads into a leggiero section that is a descending chain passing throughout the ensemble, which returns to a homorhythmic line in the ensemble for a measure before a fragmented sixteenth note motif passing around the ensemble. The movement ends with a repeated note motif with interjections in between the statements. The next movement “Vse vpered” (Ça ira) is in a lively tempo centered around a disjunct quintuplet motif. Eventually, a liscio melody sings out overtop of this texture that constantly trades off mid phrase between the clarinet, flute, and oboe. The third movement “Hazavzhdy” (Forever) is structured on alternating adagio and allegretto sections. The adagios feature lush homorhythmic chords with accelerando and ritardando beamed sixteenth notes coming in and out of the texture. The allegrettos consist of chains of small fragments that are connected through each instrument of the ensemble to create a larger phrase. Finally, the movement ends with a quirky three note motif and rests in the bassoon that the clarinet plays grace notes into the downbeats. The fourth movement “Sklyane sertse” (Glass heart) is a harpsichord variation consisting of a sequence of eighth notes that gets developed and transformed throughout, which are interrupted by subito flourishes of notes in a quasi-cadenza manner. Eventually, a more melodic line built on a sequence in an articulated and lively character is introduced. This leads to an aleatoric measure in the clarinet and bassoon to end the movement. The final movement “Zapoviyi” (Overtaken will) is a tranquillo character with lyrical contrapuntal lines that use different instrumentation pairings to express different colors in the ensemble.

description: This is a three-movement concerto that explores the main concepts of postmodernism through an exploration of timbralism. Denysenko experiments with uncommon and unusual textures of phonic and sonorous qualities of timbre through timbre modality. This concept reveals an artistic metaphor that clarifies the semantics of the work. The first movement “Erro - Blukaty Pomylyatyi’ (Wandering mistakenly)” is an energetic vivo that features an arpeggiated motif that gets developed and reinterpreted in different textures throughout, which leads into a virtuosic bassoon cadenza. Next, a moderato section imitating earlier material progresses back into a vivo. The movement ends with an aleatoric senza misura accompaniment in the orchestra while the bassoon finishes the theme ending on intense fermata multiphonic notes. The next movement “Esvilibrium geminorum - Rivnovaha blyznyukiv (Equilibrium of twins)” is a tranquillo that explores different extended techniques to manipulate timbre. It opens with a rhythmic accompaniment in the percussion while the bassoon plays long tones while singing and playing. Later glissandos are introduced into the bassoon line to expand the coloristic options, while the accompaniment gets thicker and busier. This climaxes into a senza misura section structure by second timings consisting of two technical aleatoric passages in the bassoon leading to a low E long note with frullato to conclude the piece. The final movement “Salve Rex - Tryvit tsaryu (Long live the King) is an allegretto that explores unspecified pitch beaming in the bassoon part to get a wide variety of articulations to expand the timbral possibilities. This is combined with short fragments that develop and connect as the movement progresses. This leads into another senza misura section in the orchestral accompaniment, while the bassoon plays long tones to conclude the piece

The work is built of genre combination of romance and medieval music characteristics from the hocket while utilizing timbral contrasts. It expands the coloristic capabilities of the bassoon through different elements of genre.

description: This is a short one-movement work that explores a variety of characters in a postmodernist language and style. It opens with an introduction that is a call and response between the harpsichord and bassoon. The harpsichord has rhythmic chords, while the bassoon has a syncopated arpeggiated motif or long tone multiphonics. The structure of the piece alternates between dense and thinner texture sections that require immediate character change. The denser sections often consist of an active line of sixteenth notes and chords with unexpected syncopations in the harpsichord that are combined with rhythmically energetic syncopated lines and strings of articulated sixteenths often in large intervals. The thinner sections often are more lyrical and quasi-improvisatory either in a cadenza manner or a simple accompaniment.

description: This is a three-movement work with no title indications given using aesthetics and techniques from the avant-garde movement. The first movement is marked “quarter equals 60” written in an unmetered form. It starts with the same theme presented in each of the voices that becomes different as it progresses. However, each part is written with a different amount of spacing between each note. For example, the first couple notes which are homorhythmic do not line up but rather appear like one of the parts is syncopated. Often throughout the movement the beats do not line up, for example one part will have two eighth notes and their next note of the following beat written before another voice has all three of their triplet eighth notes written. I believe this could be to indicate the players each playing the theme at their own will independently of one another creating a contrapuntal and improvisatory-like texture. The second movement has no marking or tempo indication given. It features the same elements as the previous movement except the theme begins alone in the flute with the oboe joining the second phrase and the bassoon finally on the third phrase. The movement ends with an aleatoric section with only note heads given with different amounts of spacing between the notes for each part. The final movement is marked “half note equals 54” metered in 2/2. It features a note that gets passed around the ensemble beginning as a long note value becoming shorter as the movement progresses until it becomes a sixteenth note. The movement concludes with a passage of eighth notes in large intervals.

This is a short work in ternary form that features both the technical and lyrical capabilities of the bassoon. The A section opens with an eight-measure piano introduction in e minor that introduces the first theme consisting of four slurred sixteenths in an upper and lower neighbour motion followed by four arpeggiated staccato eighth notes. The bassoon then enters playing the theme while the piano provides an accompaniment texture with staccato eighth note chords. This theme continues developing, becoming longer with more eighth notes and sixteenths added in a row in an arpeggiated manner highlighting the harmonies. Next, a seven-measure piano interlude on the first theme, which continues underneath the bassoon’s next entrance of the second theme. The second theme is more lyrical, featuring mostly dotted quarter notes with an occasional measure of an eighth and quarter note. This is contrasted phrase by phrase with material similar to the first theme. This continues to develop until a five-measure interlude in the piano that ritardandos into the B section “Poco piu sostenuto” in C major in a cantabile espressivo character. This section has similar material presented in the short second theme phrases that appeared in the previous section. The piano has an accompaniment texture with dotted quarter note chords in the right hand and an arpeggiated quarter followed by an eighth bass line in the left hand. This is followed by a return to the A section which develops the material slightly differently than in the opening.

description: This is a three-movement work that displays Dorfman’s style combining elements of avant-garde style that explores different timbres through graphic notation and multiphonics that is combined with more neoclassical motifs that are Shostakovich like and Jewish folk and religious music. The first movement is structured on a constantly changing and contrasting section. It begins with an “Allegro” unmetered section, consisting of short fragments that jump between the low and high register of the bassoon. There are notes throughout that interrupt the line with unspecified rhythm with graphic notation for vibrato. The next section “Animato cantabile” begins with a lyrical melody that begins more disjunct through larger intervals and more technical passages incorporated. A short two measure “Allegretto” section of sixteenth notes interrupts before returning to the “Andante.” Another interruption occurs in an “Animato cantabile” section of two measures consisting of septuplet sixteenth notes returning to the Andante again that develops this time into an “Animato assai” featuring material in a similar manner to the opening to conclude the movement. The second movement “Adagio” is in ternary form. It opens with a rhythmic repeated note motif that expands into a melody ornamented with grace notes that leads into unspecified rhythm notes with harmonics, trills, tremolos, and smorzato. This leads into a section with a weaving around melody that builds sequentially. Eventually, the opening material returns with ornamentation and variation. The final movement “Presto” opens with a sixteenth note motif built around the intervals of third, fourth and fifth that is repeated three times before expanding. It ascends and descends the range of the bassoon leading to a fermata low “C”. The motif returns this time staccato as opposed to slurred and expands slowly in a sequential manner. This leads into an espressivo melody built around arpeggios. Next, a couple technical passages in an aleatoric manner consisting of first large intervals and weaving around texture. This returns to the opening material with some slight variations such as a trill added at the top of passage before descending.

piece_title: Paraphase on a Ukrainian Folk Song
premiere: 2016 at NMAU by Pavlo Shevchuk (fl), Nina Bahrina (cl), Dmytro Drach (bsn)
description: This is a short one movement work that is based on the Ukrainian folk song “Oy khodyt’ son” (Oh the dream goes by) in a calm character reflecting the lullaby nature of the folk song. The piece develops the theme while reworking material to create a variety of textures throughout. The piece opens with an introduction that utilizes fragments of the melody in each of the parts that interweave together that lead into a rhythmic motif of dotted eighth followed by a sixteenth note. Next, the clarinet takes over the melody while the bassoon echoes a different part of the melody during its longer note values. The two parts weave between each other creating a constant cyclic feel of the melody. Eventually, the flute enters taking over the melodic role overtop of contrapuntal accompaniment parts in the clarinet and bassoon, which become more active as the section develops becoming a string of eighth notes. Next, the music begins to become a more agitated character with the introduction of accents and syncopation into the texture when the bassoon takes over the melody representing the intensifying of the dream. This becomes a fully contrapuntal texture, which climaxes to a fermata chord on B major allowing a reset to the original calm lullaby texture of the opening. This closing section begins with a four-note fragment of the melody in a canon around the ensemble leading to the dotted eighth and sixteenth rhythmic motif that then unwinds to the final chord that is then repeated after two beats of silence. This leads to another two beats of silence before the bassoon playing the tonic alone to conclude the work.
It was a required chamber piece for his students
He wrote various examination pieces for his students.

description: This is a four-movement suite in a style very typical of early twentieth-century French wind writing reminiscent of Paul Taffanel’s wind quintet and Darius Milhaud’s wind pieces. The first movement “Sous la feuillée” is in ternary form in an Andantino tempo marked “tres tranquillo” opens with an espressivo theme in the oboe that the flute joins in on for fragments to highlight key cadential moments, which comes back throughout the movement in new key areas and harmonies. This is overtop of accompaniment lines such as ostinato sixteenth note arpeggiation in the first bassoon and first clarinet, a bass line in the second bassoon, and drones and counter-melody in the horns. The second section “toujours tres tranquille” begins with sixteenths leading to eighth notes motif in the horns in parallel third motion, which gets passed around the ensemble. This is combined with longer note values in the rest of the ensemble providing harmonic support. This continues developing until we climax back into the original theme again. Eventually, the motif returns into the texture to help tie everything together to conclude the movement. The second movement “Radieuse matinée” marked Allegretto con grazia opening with an energetic and cantabile theme in the flute consisting of a measure of eighth and sixteenth notes leading to a longer note value combined with accompaniment figures in the ensemble. Eventually, the oboe enters with the second theme built around an arpeggiated triplet eighth note figure that rises and then meanders downwards in duple eighth notes. The texture then becomes a dialogue passing this theme around while the texture develops into more contrapuntal writing, such as having the main theme woven in. The rest of the movement continues developing and reworking this material in different textures and characters becoming more agitated as it climaxes before returning to the original dolce character. The third movement “Promenade sentimentale” is marked Allegretto non troppo utilizing a similar approach of writing taking elements of structure and styles from the previous movements such as opening with the clarinet playing the main theme with the flute joining on fragments for emphasis and typical accompaniment figures.  However, the character of the main theme is more pedantic and heavier. This is contrasted with a lively middle section “Piu vivo” with a dance-like character. The upper winds play a detached eighth note followed by two sixteenth motif overtop of rhythmic accompaniment figures such as an offbeat motif in the horn and a bass line in the bassoon. A “Lento” section in a chorale style briefly interrupts this allowing for a return to the opening character and reworking of the original material before the Piu Vivo returns. This interruption occurs again leading to a final return of the opening material to conclude the movement. The final movement “Ronde villageoise” is marked Allegro giocoso in a lively dance-like character. It consists of an energetic theme of eighth and sixteenth notes organized in a period initially played in unison by the clarinets overtop of rhythmic accompaniment figures. As it develops a more vocal-like theme is introduced in the flute, while the accompaniment becomes more virtuosic.

unpublished: handwritten manuscript located at the Provincial Archives of Alberta in Box 13 of “Eremenko Sheet Music”
key: I (G major), II (D major), III (D major)
description: This is a three-movement work in a neoclassical style using typical structure, phrasing, motifs, and idiomatic writing characteristic of wind quintet writing combined with elements of Ukrainian folk song and dance. The first movement has a ternary form. The A section “Allegro” opens with two repeated sixteenth notes leading to a long note in a canon texture in score order beginning with the horn and ending with the flute. This leads into a contrapuntal texture with each of the parts playing a variation of one another built around staccato eighth and sixteenth notes. This develops until a homorhtyhmic texture emerges in a chorale-like texture of quarter and half notes. This texture is then alternated with the contrapuntal texture. This sets up the B section “Meno mosso” that consists of a slurred and lyrical melody in the flute and oboe overtop of accompaniment figures in the rest of the ensemble. The melody then gets passed to the horn and bassoon before developing into a contrapuntal texture that prompts the return of the A material. A short coda “Vivace” section that is the opening material concludes the movement. The next movement “Andante cantabile” starts off with a folk-like vocal melody played by the horn alone. For the second phrase the clarinet enters in canon to the horn, while the bassoon enters with a countermelody. For the following the oboe and flute enter in canon briefly before switching to accompaniment figures. The movement continues developing the material getting more virtuosic until it climaxes. Then the instruments begin to drop out of the texture until the horn is left alone to finish playing the theme with grace note ornamentation now added. The final movement is built around a variety of short sections that are combined together. The first section “Allegro” has a dance-like character of syncopated melody of eighth and sixteenth notes leading to a quarter or dotted quarter note. As it develops the texture becomes more contrapuntal with virtuosic passages of sixteenth notes passing around. The next section “Meno mosso” returns the theme back to the original sparse texture, which develops in a similar fashion. The following “Moderato” is a short four-measure transition with a motif that gets passed around in score order beginning with the flute and ending with the horn. The next section “Andante” consists of a lyrical theme and accompaniment figures. The following “Allegretto” brings back the original theme in a canon-like texture that leads into an “Allegro vivo” presenting the theme in the original texture, which develops in the same fashion as before. This leads to the final “Presto” consisting of articulated sixteenth notes in the flute and oboe over top of accompaniment figures. This becomes the final phrase consisting of homorhythmic eighth notes leading to a rest. After the rest, a final motif on the tonic “D” of two sixteenths, dotted quarter tied to eighth followed by three eighth notes is played to conclude the work.

premiere: November 24th, 2023 at “Young Composers Concert” at NUCU in Kyiv by Dmytro Malin (bsn), composer (pno)
description: This is a two-movement work utilizing neoclassical forms with jazz harmonic language. Each movement is structured in two main sections. First, an “Arioso” section that features the bassoon playing solo that is attacca into a “Piece” section which has the bassoon and piano both playing where the main theme is presented and developed. The first movement’s arioso is rubato and quasi-improvised based around arpeggiations in a variety of rhythms with some influence from jazz harmony. The “Piece” is marked “Animato” beginning with the bassoon presenting a melody overtop of a driving eighth note ostinato in the left hand and interjections in the right hand when the bassoon is resting. The melody switches between moments of lyricism through slurred legato lines and humoresque through staccato eighth notes. Eventually, the roles reverse with the piano taking over the melody and the bassoon playing the ostinato eighth notes. This leads to a final two measures where the two instruments align on an eighth note arpeggiated line into a chord to conclude the movement. The second movement’s arioso is marked “Andante mosso” in a more virtuosic character featuring technical passages in scalar and arpeggiated motion combined with large intervals. The “Piece” is marked “Animato assai” and features the same texture as the previous movement. However, the melody this time is more cantabile with it being comprised of whole notes in the bassoon. This leads into a virtuosic section of sixteenth note arpeggios in dialogue between the bassoon and the right hand of the piano combined with chords in the left hand. Next, a “Moderato” section consisting of a cantabile melody in the bassoon with accompaniment figures centered around two stepwise sixteenth notes followed by a large interval eighth note in the piano. Eventually, the sixteenths and eighth note ostinato creep back in. The ostinato motif develops into sixteenths as the piece climaxes while all of the motifs interact leading to a final tonic chord.

premiere: never performed
description: The title of this work Lemon was chosen by Fedko as a cheeky play on words as the work itself sounds “sour” due to the harmonic choices utilized. This is a short one-movement work that explores different tone colors such as having the flute playing in their lower register instead of always being the highest voice in the texture. The opening section “Andante assai” begins with a dialogue between the flute in their lowest register and the oboe in their middle to higher register. Next, the clarinet enters with a countermelodic line and the bassoon with an arpeggiated bassline creating a four-voice contrapuntal texture, which continues developing until it arrives at a fermata to conclude the section. The next section “Andante mosso” consists of an interlocking accompaniment in the flute and oboe that is trading off sixteenth notes in an ostinato pattern, while the bassoon plays a lyrical melody overtop of a countermelody in the clarinet. A return to the “Andante assai” occurs but not in the original texture. The bassoon brings back its arpeggiated bassline, but the oboe emerges into a soloistic role with new melodic content while the flute in the low register and clarinet in the middle and upper register play an accompaniment in homorhythm. However, new material that is more aggressive syncopated motif being presented in homorhythm amongst the ensemble interrupts briefly for four measures. The original material returns but more active with passages of sixteenth notes in dialogue now. The following section “Andante con moto” changes character to a playful character through staccato passages of eighth and sixteenth notes that rotate around the ensemble overtop of accompaniment figures. This continues developing until its arrival a dissonant chord that intensifies and crescendos through a fermata to set up the brief coda section “Andante maestoso.” This is a five-measure chorale that explores dissonances in order to arrive at a final consonant G minor chord to conclude the work.

description: This is a five-movement suite from earlier in Fiala’s career which his style was described by Biernel as having a “warmth, astonishing intimacy of expression with a touch of humanity.” (Biernel, 20) The work reflects the composer’s fascination with Hindemith’s writing. The first movement “Allegretto con grazia” utilizes brief motifs in changing meters to create repetitive segments in a contrapuntal texture. There are three main motifs 1) two eighth notes in a descending perfect fourth that ascends a perfect fifth to a quarter note followed by three descending eighth notes, 2) two eighth notes either ascending or descending second, and 3) eighth and two sixteenths in a scalar motion. These motifs are developed by connecting into larger phrases through the interaction of the different voices. The second movement “Chant” is in a largo tempo in an ABABA form. It opens with a Ukrainian folk melody in the horn solo that is subdued and lyrical. This melody gets passed around the ensemble in a contrapuntal texture underneath. The B section is marked “piu mosso” in a more transparent texture featuring a melody divided between two instruments overtop of accompaniment figures in the rest of the ensemble. The movement explores a variety of key centers throughout. The third movement “Fugetta” has an energetic character in an allegro vivace tempo which presents a theme consisting of eighth, tied eighth, and quarter notes in a fugal texture beginning in the bassoon followed by the oboe, clarinet, horn, and finally the flute. The following movement “Intermezzo” is in a moderato espressivo tempo that takes a theme and switches it between different textures 1) homorhythmic passages, 2) trading off, and 3) solo playing. The last movement “Finale” in an allegretto pomposo tempo. This movement also takes a couple motifs that are developed and fragmented through variations and changes to texture such as contrapuntal, trading off and cannon entry like an echo as it progresses. The main motif in this movement is two ascending eighth notes to a dotted eighth note that descends to a sixteenth and eighth note. However, as it progresses the direction and intervals change. Overall, this work demonstrates Fiala’s rejection of avant-garde idioms. It shows his preference for classical forms and influence of Ukrainian folk music with transparent textures, harmonic dissonance, and incisive rhythms.

description: This is a four-movement suite in a neoromantic style with elements and inspiration from folklorism. Overall, the work can be characterized by its logical structure with melodic lines that are lyrical and expressive combined with moments of dissonance to create tension. The instrumentation choices throughout provide colorful and rich contrasts. The first movement “Moderato marciale” in the form of ABACABC presents an opening theme in a march style featuring dotted eighth and sixteenth rhythms split between the first clarinet and oboe overtop of ostinato chords in the horns. As it develops the whole ensemble becomes involved becoming more contrapuntal such as a line of triplets trading between the bassoons and fragmentation echoing the theme. This leads into a secondary section marked “cantando” that is more lyrical overtop of chordal writing in the accompaniment. As the section develops the triplet fragment from the first section is introduced into the texture setting up a return to the A section. Next, another contrasting section occurs in a legato character and more transparent texture consisting of a melody, downbeat chords, and a bass line. The following movement “Berceuse” in an Andante quasi adagio tempo presents a folk-like melody beginning in the first clarinet solo. Slowly the other instruments enter with each successive part being more active allowing the texture to become thicker. For example, the horns enter first with a half note slurred to a quarter note motif and eventually ending with an eighth note ostinato in the first bassoon. Throughout the movement different accompaniment figures are presented to change the character and texture. The third movement “Scherzino” is in an Allegretto con grazia tempo and has an energetic dance-like character presenting a theme based around sixteenth notes overtop of accompaniment and ostinato figures and motifs. The final movement “Finale” has three main sections 1) Maestoso, 2) Andantino con moto, and 3) Allegro. The first section is an introduction setting up the main theme to come with fragments from it in a regal character. The next section begins with a full presentation of the main theme first in the oboe in a giocoso character with accompaniment figures rotating around the ensemble. Eventually, a secondary theme and countermelody are presented in a cannon texture. This leads to a reprise of the introduction section that gets expanded and switches between moments of contrapuntal and homorhythmic writing until the earlier material emerges. The final section is a short coda presenting the opening material in a faster tempo.

description: This is a three-movement work utilizing elements of sonata form combined with a fusion of influences. Fischer’s music often takes inspiration and combines a large amount of influences into his own unique voice. The common influences in his music are his roots incorporating elements of traditional Jewish, Slavic folk music, South American dance music combined with classical influences of French impressionism, Hindemith, and occasionally modernist techniques such as twelve-tone, serialism, and avant-garde. This results in a style that oscillates between styles utilizing polyphonic lines that are interwoven with harsh polyharmony. The first movement “Allegro” is in sonata form opening with a march-like introduction in the piano consisting of a staccato eighth note followed by an eighth rest combined with a dotted eighth and sixteenth. The bassoon enters solo playing an energetic main theme composed of staccato eighth and sixteenth melody leading to long notes, which the march-like occurs underneath. This continues developing with the piano becoming more active with passages of sixteenth notes. As the section continues it is contrasted with a lyrical and vocal-like melody in the bassoon, while continuing in the energetic and staccato character. The second theme is a meno mosso in a more lyrical and calm character in a contrapuntal texture. The development takes fragments from the opening as its basis. This leads back to a full recapitulation that goes attacca into the second movement which is in a cantabile character in ternary form. The A section “Andante” presents a folk-like melody that uses more impressionistic harmonic choices. The B section “Piu mosso” has a sequential two slurred sixteenth note pattern that ascends and descends overtime underneath a vocal-like melody. The return of the A section brings back the opening theme with a new accompaniment texture. In the opening it was chordal and in the return it is more contrapuntal. The movement ends with an accelerando in the piano to attacca into the final movement also in ternary form. The A section “Allegro” has a dance-like character with a lively eighth and sixteenth note theme in the bassoon that is mainly in scalar or arpeggiated motion, often with a lower neighbour motion. The piano plays accompaniment figures and takes over the theme while the bassoon rests. The B section “Meno mosso” features a cantabile slurred theme in the bassoon overtop of chordal accompaniment in the piano. The section accelerandos back into the A material with a much more active piano accompaniment. This is interrupted by a short eight measure “Meno mosso” piano interlude in a chorale-style. The A material returns again with the cantabile theme being incorporated this time leading to a eight measure tutti quarter note chordal passage to an unexpected a B minor augmented 5th chord to conclude the work.
