description: This is a seven-movement suite in a neorenaissance style featuring elements typical of this style such as steady beat, balanced phrases, and polyphony. The first movement “Corale” is in a slow tempo featuring four-voice polyphony in an imitative style. The voices weave in and out of one another with a few moments of clarity when the voices are moving in similar rhythmic motion. For example, at rehearsal 2, two of the voices have two quarter notes followed by a tied half note while the other two voices have a dotted half note followed by two eighth notes. The second movement “Ricercare” is imitative and contrapuntal in a medium tempo. Each of the voices enter separately beginning with the second bassoon, followed by the first, then the third, and finally ending with the fourth. The third movement “Contrappunto” is a slow contrapuntal movement when each of the parts enter separately with a slight variation of the melody in order to follow practices of renaissance polyphony. The fourth movement “Caccia” features the voices in canon in a strict melodic imitation at the perfect fifth beginning with the second bassoon starting on Bb, followed by the third on F, the fourth on C, and finally the first on G. The fifth movement “Contrappunto” is reminiscent of the earlier one utilizing motifs from it in a different order and combination of polyphony. The sixth movement “Canzone” is a very slow, legato song-like character. It features a lyrical melody in the first bassoon, an accompaniment ostinato two slurred eighth note motif in the second and third bassoon, and a bass line in the fourth. The final movement “Motetto” is a polyphonic texture. The opening has each of the voices entering separately on an independent line each moving on their own while the other voices have a note of a longer value. Throughout there are brief moments where certain voices will align in homophonic polyphony, for example two measures before rehearsal 2 in second and third bassoon. Eventually, the movement ends with a section of imitative polyphony where triplet sixteenths are echoed throughout the ensemble.

description: This is a one-movement work in an avant-garde style. Hodziatsky was a prominent member of the Kyiv Avant-Garde, and this work follows in his style from that period. His music often takes inspiration from both the neoclassical style of Stravinsky combined with Western Second Viennese and avant-garde composers. Hodziatsky declared against the use of dodecaphony within his work, which was common in the serial music of the time. The work begins with a sixteenth note fragment in the flute overtop of staccato quarter note at the start of each fragment in the oboe and clarinet. This develops into a longer and cohesive line in the flute overtop of long notes that change and weave in and out of one another in the ensemble. Slowly, the accompaniment becomes more active and independent creating a contrapuntal texture eventually, becoming a canon-like texture of the line in the flute. This material winds down into a rhythmic and contrapuntal duet between the horn and the bassoon. Gradually, the ensemble joins back one at the time beginning with the clarinet followed by the oboe. The introduction of the flute denotes a new section “Meno mosso” featuring a theme in the flute overtop of trilled long notes changing at different times throughout the ensemble, which were set up at the end of the previous section to create a seamless transition between the sections. Motifs from earlier in the piece are brought back into the flute overtop of this texture before returning to the original meno mosso material. Eventually, the accompaniment texture changes to tutti chords with the occasional dialogue during the flute’s longer note values. As this progresses the oboe as juxtaposition to this legato and calm texture with material from the beginning section as interruptions that develop into a full line. This leads into a contrapuntal duet of the flute and oboe playing this earlier material, which the clarinet joins in for a while before returning to a duet. Later on the clarinet, bassoon, and horn re-enter with the chorale-like accompaniment again underneath the flute and oboe’s contrapuntal staccato sixteenth lines. A final return to the duet texture returns this time winding down into motifs from the calmer sections in dialogue to conclude the work.

description: This is a two-movement concerto with each structured in an alternation of slow and fast sections displaying many character changes throughout. The work utilizes elements of Ukrainian folk melody, tonality, and dance combined with elements of neoromanticism such as harmonic language and structures. The concerto is dedicated to bassoonist Oleksandr Lytyvnov, who I assumed would have premiered the work in the mid-1970s. The first movement opens with an “Allegro non troppo” opens with a main theme consisting of repeated eighth notes with scalar passages to change harmonies in the bassoon overtop of rhythmically driven chords. As the section develops the melody displaces the notes into different octaves to sound more disjunct. Another variation for the second half occurs turning the rhythm into a syncopation creating more forward momentum. The slow section “Andante” features a lyrical folk-like melody in the bassoon based around eighth, quarter, and dotted quarter notes leading to longer note values overtop of accompaniment figures in the piano. There is also a third staff inserted in the piano throughout with a countermelody line while the bassoon plays longer note values. A short bassoon cadenza in a con animo character presenting scalar material connects into a meno mosso section in a funebre character that presents a eighth note melody that weaves around in the bassoon overtop of chords in an syncopated ostinato in the left hand and counter melody in the right hand. A return to the opening section occurs but starting in the second half of the opening section. This continues developing such as adding virtuosic chromatic sextuplets to connect the harmony changes. This leads into another short bassoon cadenza consisting of a descending eighth note line followed by a group of four thirty-second notes slurred into long notes. Next, an orchestral interlude in a “moderato” tempo occurs bringing back material from the slower sections. A final “Allegro” section occurs featuring a virtuosic double tonguing passage that is in dialogue with the piano. The second movement opens with an “Allegro molto” section beginning with the piano playing a fragmentation that develops adding more of the main theme until finally achieving a full presentation of it. The bassoon then enters playing the dance-like theme overtop of the original fragmentation in the piano until the bassoon arrives at an unexpected low B♭ fermata half note. This prompts a restarting of the theme with a rhythmic ostinato added to the left hand. The solo material and accompaniment continues getting more active and thicker orchestration until arriving at our perfect cadence. Next, an “Andante” section occurs featuring rolled chords in the piano with a vocal-like melody in the bassoon. Eventually, a counter melody is introduced underneath the bassoon’s long notes. A return to the “Allegro molto” material occurs. Afterwards new material is introduced such as a disjunct eighth note passage that always begins on the second eighth note of the measure in the bassoon. This leads into a “Moderato” piano interlude similar to the first movement’s interlude. Finally, the main and largest bassoon cadenza occurs. It is in a virtuosic manner featuring large articulated intervals, trills, and slurred chromatic scalar passages. A shortened reprise of the opening material occurs again leading into a short “Piu mosso” section with motifs from the opening to conclude the concerto.

description: This is a one-movement work that is based on mikromotyvy, which are rhythmic and melodic motifs that are generated by algorithms through independent combinatory systems. The material for these motifs ranges from three to seven notes in length originating from one of the 518 songs by folk singer Yavdokha Zuyikha. Her collection of songs were published in Ukraine and became a source for many of Hrabovsky’s works. These motifs are superimposed on a completely different rhythmic canvas, constructed by the composer. These quotes from the folk songs are not used in a typical fashion as expected in classical music. Hrabovsky uses the interval of the melodic movement that is inherent in Ukrainian musical folklore but transferred to a distinctive rhythmic context. Therefore, everything is dictated by controlled random processes placed in certain frames, which their combinations ensure the fluidity and variability of the musical flow. The overall structure of the piece is based on the system of mikromotyvy linking together smaller portions of the pitch and rhythmic material as the building blocks to create larger structures, which generate new pitch material and rhythmic patterns to be derived from for the next section. This also determines the timbral qualities through the interplay of foreground and background texture between the melodic lines and polyphonic harmony. Throughout the piece five different types of backgrounds are utilized that link together the various algorithms that create a total of thirty different timbral variations. Each section has its own instrumentation based on a number series that differentiates the form. Eventually, this creates a three-part canon in the foreground that changes polyphonic textures. Overall, this work creates a unique approach to form through combining algorithmic systems with folk elements and polyphony in an avant-garde musical language.

description: Original title is “From Japanese Haiku” [З японських гоку] but the title was changed due to confusion between the similarity of the number 3 with the word «з». This is a six-movement suite based on Japanese haikus using a variety of avant-garde elements to structure the piece to create new and unexpected textures. This work was written during the period of Hrabovsky’s career when he was involved as a member of the Kyiv avant-garde. Joel Spiegelman received a copy of the score to bring back to the United States when he met Hrabovsky on a visit to Kyiv in 1965. The work is structured using free notation without any meter but rather events or short motifs that the players respond to combined with aleatoric moments in order to create a larger form. Harmonically, this work achieves to create its own language through contrasting and combining different elements of atonal and modal pitch sequences throughout. This is also combined with different approaches to timbre through the manipulation of extended techniques and non-pitched noises with irregular moments of clusters and extremely rapid passages emerging from the texture to create a different sonic world for each movement. The first movement “The Butterfly’s Wings” is an alternating phrase by phrase duet between the piccolo and the tenor exploring different timbres with frullato in the piccolo and Flatterzunge in the tenor. The second movement “In the Dead of the Night '' has a motif that jumps back and forth between the xylophone and tenor that develops into one line in the tenor overtop of a double tongued aleatoric texture in the piccolo. The next movement “And fields and Mountains” features a staccato eighth note melody overtop of long tones in the piccolo and muted bassoon that unexpectedly leads into a rapid passage of notes in the piccolo. The fourth movement “On the tooth of the mountain” is the only time in the piece that the entire ensemble is playing and interacting together with weaving aleatoric passages combining to create a thick and active texture. The next movement “How Still is the Garden” features short phrases in the tenor overtop of long tones in the bassoon and xylophone that briefly become active to assist with the phrase through fragmentation. The final movement “Shudder Distant Hills” is a duet between the tenor and bassoon. It opens with a dialogue of a three accented eighth note motif leading to a long note symbolized through unconventional notation of a black line until the next event, which is utilized throughout the entire piece for long tones. However, the exploration occurs through the use of a multiphonic in the bassoon. After the opening section, a legato melody is presented through alternating each note between the tenor and bassoon. This climaxes into the opening motif returning in unison to conclude the work.

description: This is a five-movement work that combines elements of neoclassical structure with avant-garde aesthetics and language. It was written after a twenty-year break from composing. The first movement “Scandalous Squabble” is marked very fast using an avant-garde atonal language that is structured around the combination of multiphonic long tones that often enter syncopated and a constant line of disjunct sixteenths that involve a pattern of chromatic intervals often displaced by an octave with perfect fifths that pass around the ensemble. This effect creates constantly changing textures and timbres through the different pairing of instrumentations. Eventually, a 7:4 motif of half notes and quarter notes is introduced that interrupts this chain leading to a cadenza moment in the horn consisting of a large descending glissando to conclude the movement. The next movement “Funeral Interrupted” is marked molto largo, alla marcia funebre structured in a more neoclassical approach. It consists of a typical rhythmic ostinato of quarter, dotted eighth, and sixteenth note in the flute, clarinet, horn, and bassoon that keeps the momentum moving forward. This motif is often in cluster chords rather than the expected minor tonality of a marcia funebre. However, as the work develops this motif expands to have the eighth note and sixteenth three times in a row before returning to a quarter note. Overtop of this texture is a singing, legato oboe solo that plays around with the rhythmic motif often creating syncopation with the accompaniment. The third movement “Supra-Florid Counterpoint” is marked molto largo in a contrapuntal texture. It features five independent lines in an atonal language that are weaving in and out of one another often creating rhythmic dissonance through the combination of different note groupings occurring at the same time such as 3:5 and 4:3 overlapping. The movement has a legato and calm character through tenutos and long slur markings that gets thrown off by the rhythmic dissonance. The next movement “Scattered Mozaic” is marked allegro volatile consists of short fragments that are different rhythmically and pitch-wise in each instrument that connect together to create a larger cohesive phrase. The texture is thinner, usually consisting of only one or briefly two instruments playing at a time when fragments overlap. The final movement “Intimate Chant” is marked lentissimo is homophonic line in the ensemble consisting of longer note values, mainly half notes and whole notes often tied over the bar lines to create a metrical ambiguity. This is combined with the occasional moment of quarter notes to bring a moment of metrical clarity.

description: This is a one-movement concerto-like work that alternates between sections of monologue in the bassoon with orchestral accompaniment that bridges different sections together. Hubarenko’s musical process for this work can be perceived as a free improvisation unfolding toward the final figurative synthesis through powerful dynamic waves to form linear momentum. He combines this with an excellent knowledge of orchestral colors to enhance his lyrical dramatic style similar to Samuel Barber and Vaughn Williams. The work opens with a “Sostenuto” section that features a lyrical line that becomes more disjunct with larger intervals as it becomes more rhythmical active from duple to triplet eighth notes. After it unwinds to a whole note on the pitch “Bb” the orchestra enters in unison on this pitch as it weaves around becoming more tonally ambiguous leading to a cluster chord, which another monologue in the bassoon emerges from. This pattern continues of the orchestra entering in unison at the end of the phrase and becoming more ambiguous. Eventually, a rhythmic ostinato on the pitch “B♭” of dotted eighth note and sixteenth note leading to a quarter note that is tied the first time and untied the second time. As it progresses it builds to become a cluster chord as the bassoon plays a melodic line overtop. This leads into the second section “Andante cantabile” with a vocal-like line in the bassoon overtop of a drone, running line of eighth notes, and countermelody. This eventually develops into another short monologue leading back to the opening orchestral interlude. The next main section “Allegro non troppo” has a waltz-like character with a slurred melodic line in the bassoon overtop of a syncopated bass line. As it develops a countermelody is introduced in the upper strings that merges into a character shift in the accompaniment with a weaving eighth note line that creates a more rigid character. The melody continues expanding climaxing to a high E in the bassoon held for three measures. Afterwards, the bassoon joins this new character with a melody based off the motifs introduced by the orchestra earlier in the section. This winds down material from earlier that finds its way back to the home pitch of “B♭” to conclude the movement on a low B♭ in the bassoon that is held for four measures as the orchestra sets up a final cadence consisting of the lower strings playing B♭ that is unsettled with a B-natural in the first violin to conclude the work.

description: In Ishchenko’s music he continues the traditions of Lyatoshynsky and Shtoharenko incorporated in his own unique style that often intertwines elements from folklorism, avant-garde and modernism. This is a two-movement concerto. The first movement “Adagietto” opens with an orchestral introduction with long lines that develop into more melodic content overtop of lush harmonies in the strings. Each statement a solo wind emerges first beginning with a two-note fragment in the flute that gets elongated with each statement with the oboe then the clarinet. This finally passes off to the bassoon who finally presents the main theme. The orchestra slowly returns to the texture with accompaniment figures underneath the bassoon’s lyrical line. This develops into a dialogue texture with the winds in response over the bassoon longer note values. The next section “Poco piu mosso” has a slow waltz-like character with a quarter note melody mainly in arpeggiated and scalar motion overtop of chords and short accompaniment motifs in the orchestra. As the phrase develops, the bassoon melody quickens to a beats two and three eighth note motif in a two and two slurred note grouping. The texture then becomes small virtuosic passages in a quasi-cadenza style in dialogue with fragmented motifs from earlier in the orchestra. Eventually, all of these ideas combine together. The movement continues in this manner exploring these textures more while providing new variations on the material. The second movement “Allegro risoluto” has an energetic character in an unbalanced dance-like manner created through tied eighth notes throwing off the flow of passages of eighth notes. This is combined with accent eighth note to create a syncopated feel throughout creating rhythmic dissonance for the 6/8 metre. The texture often has a technical and virtuosic bassoon line featuring staccato eight notes in large intervals overtop of rhythmic accompaniment figures in the orchestra or a lyrical bassoon line overtop of disjunct staccato eighth notes in the orchestra. These soloistic moments are contrasted with short orchestral interludes or dialogue. Eventually, a large bassoon cadenza occurs consisting of technical and virtuosic passages exploring a wide variety of rhythmic groupings from triplet quarter notes to quintuplet sixteenth notes while exploring the full range of the bassoon. This is a three-movement concerto in a neoclassical style that borrows some elements from modernist aesthetics. The first movement “Allegretto giocoso” begins with an orchestral introduction that becomes more active and intense as the voices build on top of one another to become more contrapuntal. Eventually, the flute and bassoon enter with the theme in a dialogue passing off to each other in two measure sections that then become more fragmented as it develops. The material features syncopated and technical material presented earlier in the introduction. As this section continues it is contrasted with more lyrical and legato lines based off arpeggiation but displaced into larger intervals. The orchestra provides rhythmic support underneath creating more energy with syncopated motifs. Later, the flute and bassoon become more contrapuntal allowing both the staccato and lyrical motifs to coexist simultaneously which leads into homorhythmic passages. Eventually, a large bassoon cadenza occurs in a virtuosic manner using large interval staccato notes and grace notes typical in bassoon writing. Next, a virtuosic flute cadenza occurs featuring fiery and flourishing technical sextuplet passages. The movement then ends with a return to earlier material in contrapuntal texture that becomes homorhythmic to conclude the movement. The second movement “Andante sostenuto” features lyrical melodies that the soloists take turns performing overtop of accompaniment figures in the orchestra. As the movement develops the lyrical lines become more virtuosic and disjunct leading into a dialogue of fragments between the soloists to create one large line. The orchestra becomes more active with triplet eighth notes underneath. The rest of the moment combines the different motifs together to occur simultaneously contrasted with homorhythmic sections. The final movement “Allegro distinto” features lots of the same textures and elements from throughout the concerto with new material that is in a similar character and manner.

This is a six-movement suite that combines elements of folk song and dance. Each movement is a different type of Ukrainian folk song. The first movement “Vesnianka” are traditionally sung acapella by young women for games and dances. These songs were originally used to wake nature from its winter sleep, usually depicting new life through bird symbolism. They often have two choruses, the first representing calling the birds and the second identifying the speaker with the birds.42 This movement is in a moderato con moto tempo consisting of a theme in folk-like manner that passes around the ensemble while undergoing variations overtop of accompaniment figures, such frullato eighth notes in the flute that I believe emulate birds. Eventually, the texture becomes more contrapuntal as the theme entrances become closer together and the accompaniment material develops to become more active. The second movement “Hayivka” is in a allegro con spirito tempo that begins with a two-measure motif consisting of two beats of sixteenth notes leading to two eighth notes followed by a quarter note in the bassoon. This is followed by a canon-like texture of a two-note motif descending perfect fourth motif. These motifs come back throughout alternated with contrasting material that is more lyrical with accompaniment figures. The third movement “Rusal’na” is marked sostenuto and consists of a lyrical and folk-like melody with accompaniment figures that become more active and independent as the movement develops. The following movement “Obzhynkova” is a harvest song in an allegro fresco tempo. It begins with a homorhythmic passage of quarter and eighth notes. It then shifts to a texture of a solo melodic line with energetic fragments of eighth notes underneath. Next, a canon-like texture of the melodic content occurs that a contrapuntal texture emerges out of. The next movement “Shchedrivka” is a song for winter solstice featuring a lyrical folk-like melody again with fragmented accompaniment motifs that pass around the ensemble underneath the melody. This texture slowly becomes more contrapuntal overtime. This goes attacca into the final movement “Vesnianka” which brings back the material from the first movement.

description: This concerto explores the technical and lyrical capabilities that the bassoon is able to express through fiery articulated passages contrasted with vocal-like melodies. The motif continues to expand chromatically upwards as the orchestration thickens until a diminished fifth motif is introduced by the English horn prompting some contrapuntal writing to occur before a melody is introduced in the bassoon. This melody continues developing until it arrives at the climax of large interval slurred eighth notes, which hands off the melody to the horns for an orchestral interlude. Eventually, the bassoon re-enters in unison with the horns on the melody before taking over a soloistic role again. This leads to a short cadenza moment of a descending scalar passage in the bassoon that is separated into two parts by a pizzicato chord in the orchestra. This leads into the next main section “Piu mosso” that features a more virtuosic weaving around staccato triplet eighth note line in the bassoon overtop of a dotted eighth and sixteenth motif introduced in the orchestra. This motif in the orchestra begins in dialogue but gradually over time dominates the soloist as their material changes to repeated note triplets. Next, a return to a more mysterious character occurs with a lyrical oboe solo setting up a slower and more lyrical line in the bassoon. This develops and intensifies until arriving at another short cadenza moment similar to earlier, which leads into a longer cadenza moment. This leads to another short cadenza moment. Next, a return to a more lyrical melody in the bassoon overtop of accompaniment figures in the orchestra occurs, which like early continues to develop, intensify and thicken in orchestration until arriving at the penultimate and virtuosic page-long cadenza the music has been waiting for. This movement features a stately theme played by the bassoon that is light and staccato in nature comprised mainly of quarter and eighth notes. Combined with accompaniment figures in the piano. Throughout the movement there are subtle shifts from major to minor briefly. The movement incorporates more modern harmonic choices by exploring a range of keys through such as C major, A major and F# major. The next movement “Rigadon” is in an allegro tempo resembling the English folk dance contra dance in three main sections. This movement has a simple and lively character through a melody of arpeggiated staccato eighth notes aiming towards quarter notes combined with two sixteenth note pickups to lead into the next phrase. The piano accompaniment mainly utilizes rhythmic chords often in an ostinato pattern. The first section is in a two part form of two periods with a repetition of the second one. The theme is presented in a homophonic texture in a tonic-dominant harmonic relationship. The next section “Meno mosso” contrasts the major theme with a new theme in minor through three phases that are developed. First, the new theme is presented in two sentences. This is followed by the fragmentation of the material. Finally, material from the first theme appears in four measure phrases. Then an abbreviated reprise of the A section occurs. The final movement “Gigue” is also in an allegro tempo in ternary form. This movement is inspired and depicts the popular character Robin Hood. This movement has a fun and playful character through the dotted eighth and sixteenth note motif in an ascending sequential motion creates an energetic momentum to the music. It opens with a stately motif that is comprised of a pick-up note to a long note in the bassoon combined with chordal responses from the piano during long notes. This develops and becomes more active until it becomes a whole phrase of triplet notes. Eventually, this is briefly interrupted by a more cantabile and legato section of quarter note triplets. The texture consists of constant quarters in an arpeggiated manner in the piano with a more melodic line in the bassoon. It then returns to the original material that becomes more active and virtuosic developing into lines of articulated sixteenth notes. The next main section features the bassoon playing a repeated triplet note bass line while the piano plays a quarter note melody overtop. The next movement “Passacaglia” is in an andante commodo tempo is a vocal-like melody in the bassoon that goes under slight variations throughout such as becoming augmented or syncopated overtop of a contrast eighth note weaving line in the right hand and chords in the left hand of the piano. The final movement “Rondo - Scherzo” is in an allegro grazioso tempo. It opens with solo bassoon presenting a lilting and dance-like theme built around staccato eighth notes that descend a major third, ascends diminished fourth, and finally a minor second to a quarter note before a quasi-scalar line. The next main section is a more melodic scalar line in the bassoon overtop of chords in the piano. Eventually, this becomes fragmented and the line trades off every few notes between the two instruments leading back to the A material. description: This is a three-movement programmatic suite that combines elements of traditional and modernist writing. It is in a neo impressionist style with some Spanish folk influence that depicts the composer’s travels and experience in Spain. The first movement “Bells in Twilight” is in an Andante con moto tempo in a ternary form. It reflects a tranquil picturesque evening filled with the sound of distant church bells. The movement is centered around inventive sonorous effects to imitate bells. The A section features accented long tones entering independently throughout the ensemble that occasionally come together creating a layering effect. The meter changes every measure creating an improvisatory nature as if the bells are happening unexpectedly to the listener. The B section “Piu mosso” uses double imitation of a theme that begins as quarter notes and progresses to sixteenths and eventually, tremolos and trills. The movement concludes with an abbreviated reprise of the A section that introduces frullato into the texture. The second movement “Evening Dance” is in an Allegro tempo with a fiery character that utilizes a rhythmic motif of eighth, two sixteenth, four eighths from Coblas, humorous Spanish songs, that is combined with new, modern melodies. In this movement the horn leads the main theme in its upper register. The movement opens with a short homorhythmic introduction of trills and a descending scalar passage before introducing the rhythmic motif and dance elements in a light and staccato character. The final movement “Sounds at Midnight '' is in an Adagio tempo imitating the enchanting sounds of nature at midnight. This is achieved through pedal effects, alternation of solo episodes with tutti ensemble passages, and registrar contrast of melody and accompaniment. The bassoon’s solo episodes reproduces the lyrical atmosphere of a Spanish serenade.

description: This is a one-movement work that incorporates elements from various styles such as rhythmic and melodic motifs of folklorism, neoclassical elements of structure and contemporary aesthetics such as rhythmic dissonance of triple and duple subdivisions occurring together. The work opens with a “Rubato” section that consists of a clarinet cadenza overtop of a C drone in the left hand of the piano. Eventually, the bassoon enters in a dialogue with a counter-melody as the piano develops into a chordal texture that is metrically syncopated moving on beats 2 and 4. This leads into the next section “Allegro” features an ostinato eighth note jumping between octaves on the note C in the left hand and a quarter note melody based on the Ukrainian minor scale in the right hand of the piano. Eventually, the clarinet takes over this melody before a variation appears in the bassoon before becoming a bass line. This gives rise to a more active and virtuosic section of arpeggiated passages that are offset by an eighth note in the clarinet and bassoon overtop of chords in the piano. As this section progresses the piano becomes more involved with a syncopated rhythm with dissonance of quarter note triplets and eventually sextuplet eighths overtop of the eighth notes occurring in the winds. This leads to a contrasting “Andante” section that presents a syncopated melody through the use of tied notes, which is first given in the piano alone that the clarinet takes over followed by the bassoon in a contrapuntal manner. This leads into a virtuosic cadenza-like duet between the winds that explores the upper registers. Finally, a return to the opening texture of a drone in the piano and melody in the bassoon occurs. This section brings in different variations than the opening. This leads into a final Allegro that recombines prior material in new ways.

description: This is a four-movement suite in a neoclassical style that explores both the humoresque and lyrical side of the bassoon, while often utilizing two voice-part writing. The first movement “Allegretto” is centered around a dotted sixteenth followed by a thirty-second note in an ascending interval motif. Throughout the movement this material is expanded into longer phrases. It develops into a section of two-part voice writing with third fourth eighth note of each measure leading to the downbeat in dialogue with two eighth notes in middle of the measure to create one cohesive line. A short return to the opening material occurs leading into another contrasting section of triplet eighth notes in scalar and arpeggiate motion that develops into two-part voice writing of large intervals between the two lines. A final return to the opening material occurs to conclude the movement. The next movement “Tempo di menuetto” features typical rhythmical and melodic motifs of classical waltzes. Throughout the melodic and accompaniment lines are differentiated through two-part voice writing. The third movement “Largo” begins with a vocal like fragment that gets expanded and becomes more virtuosic that leads into an accelerando prompting an Allegro section. This section consists of a return of the first movement’s opening motif now in a virtuosic manner utilizing a two-part voice style. A return to the opening material occurs but now more active using a two-voice part style. The final movement “Allegro” has an energetic dance-like character that features passages of eighth notes leading to a string of sixteenth notes. This is contrasted with material from earlier throughout the work that are recombined and varied in new ways such as inserting elements of the first movement into the main theme of this movement or using material from the largo in a moderato tempo now.

description: This is a one movement work with four main sections that combines elements of folklorism in a fantasia style. The work opens with a cadenza in a very improvisatory manner featuring virtuosic passages traversing throughout the range of the instrument. The next section “Moderato” is an energetic dance featuring sequential passages of staccato sixteenth and eigth notes ornamented with grace notes and triplet sixteenth or duple thirty-second notes to create a folk-like character. As it develops a rhythmic motif of dotted eigth followed by a sixteenth note is introduced adding more momentum into the phrase. Next, a “Meno mosso” section takes the theme from the previous section and develops it into a virtuosic passage of constant thirty-second notes. This is followed by a short “A tempo” section that makes the theme disjunct by inverting it into larger intervals. The final section brings back the dotted rhythmic motif from earlier combined with elements from the cadenza-like opening, which leads into a “Largamento” providing one final improvisatory statement to conclude the work.

recordings: YouTube: 1) 2015 in Kharkiv by Denys Verbin (ob), Maksym Mikailov (cl), Dmytro Novytskyi (bsn) (https://youtu.be/sPdHUeIkZTA?si=hXKpPyyF-gdO-Pdc&t=70)
description: This is a three-movement work in a folklorist style using elements from Ukrainian fairy tales as inspiration behind the character of each movement. The first movement “Fairy Clock” is in a moderato tempo opening with the main motif of the movement of descending quarter notes first an octave followed by diminished fifth that are two slurred and two tongued, which leads into the second motif of three eighth notes. It first appears as three repeated notes beginning on the beat but gets transformed to become a syncopated ascending chromatic line. It then continues to undergo various variations throughout the movement. Often the bassoon has bass line figures that feature elements from the main motif but in different variations such as ascending. The movement continues by providing variations on these motifs with the introduction of new material such as arpeggiated eigth notes in the clarinet. The next movement “Music Box” is in an andantino tempo and opens with a contrapuntal texture. It features a lyrical melody with moments of humoresque with staccato eighth notes in the oboe, a playful ostinato consisting of two slurred sixteenths leading to two eighth notes, and a syncopated bass line in the bassoon. This develops into the bassoon taking over the lyrical melodic role, while the oboe and clarinet play the rhythmic ostinato on a repeated note creating a more march-like character. Eventually, a return to the opening material and texture occurs with some variation in the melody by ornamentation of sixteenth notes in the line. This leads into an oboe cadenza in an improvisatory manner leading to a long note, in which the clarinet and bassoon play one final statement of their opening material underneath to conclude the movement. The final movement “Buffoonery” is in an allegro tempo with a Rondo form. It opens with the same texture of the previous movement. The oboe has the melodic material that switches between lyrical and energetic staccato passages overtop of quarter notes in the clarinet and a bass line in the bassoon. The next section consists of fragmented eighth notes that trade between the instruments to create a larger cohesive line. A return to the opening material occurs with some more material added in the clarinet accompaniment line. Next, another contrasting section occurs with more fragmentation of material such as two slurred sixteenth notes combining together in a energetic character. Eventually, the fragments create a full passage by leading to staccato eighth note between each of them. The next contrasting section has a lyrical melodic line in the oboe overtop of the three-note repeated motif from earlier in the work in the clarinet and quarter notes on beats one and three in the bassoon. This develops into a syncopated rhythmic ostinato in the clarinet and bassoon. The following contrasting section utilizes fragmentation of material again. The final contrasting section combines elements from the past sections together creating a synthesis of the material to set up the final A section leading to a short six-measure coda to conclude the work.

piece_title: Variations on a Theme by Karabyts

description: This work is a theme and four variations on Ukrainian composer Ivan Karabyts (1945–2002) Piano Prelude no. 8. The work opens with four measures of an ostinato of dotted eighth and two sixteenths on the pitch “F#” followed by a dotted eighth rest in the bassoon. The two clarinets then join with the theme in rhythmic unison mostly in contrary motion in a staccato and accented manner. The first variation “Allegro” continues the dotted eighth and sixteenth part of the ostinato now with no rest between iterations in the second clarinet. The first clarinet and bassoon play elements of theme in a dialogue between the two in a risoluto character. The first clarinet has more staccato eighth note responses to a more lyrical bassoon statement consisting of a long note, rhythmic ostinato motif leading to quarter notes. Eventually, the second clarinet and bassoon switch roles. This leads into a homorhythmic passage alternating between the ostinato motif and fragments of the theme. The second variation “Adagio Sostenuto” is in a more chorale character in a contrapuntal texture consisting of quarter notes leading to half and whole notes. The third variation “Andante cantabile” features the theme now in a vocal-like line that is passed around the ensemble overtop of other contrapuntal lines such as a scalar bass line. The final variation “Andante non troppo” brings back the original character of the theme but now with rests inserted within the phrase and ornamentation of sixteenths. This is overtop of constant eighth notes on the pitch “F” switching back and forth between the low and middle octave in the bassoon. As it develops other notes are introduced based on the harmonic progression. Eventually, the bassoon switches to playing sixteenth notes in the inserted rests of the clarinet’s line. A return to the original texture of this variation occurs to conclude the movement.

description: This is a one-movement work with four main sections that reappear throughout in various reiterations in an avant-garde style that explores extended techniques possible on the bassoon combined with virtuosic moments. The first main section “Allegretto” consists of a disjointed theme of staccato eighth notes in large intervals in utilizing twelve tone that rhythmically follows the pattern of note, rest, three notes, two rests. The piano first initially enters with long tones but then joins playing the same row in canon to the bassoon line. The next main section “Allegro barbaro” consists of a sixteenth motif that is in dialogue between the bassoon and piano with accented fragmented interjections throughout. Eventually, this develops in a eighth note with a grace note motif overtop of sixteenths in a scalar motion. The following section “Meno mosso” features a dolce theme that consists of a quarter note that pitch bends a quarter tone flat into an eighth note followed by an arpeggiated group of notes in various groupings such as quintuplet, sextuplet, and nonuplet. The piano in the right hand echoes the theme displaced by a quarter note from the bassoon, while the left-hand plays chords. A reprise of the opening material returns in the piano while the bassoon plays multiphonics. Then, the bassoon joins into the opening theme in cannon to the piano. However, the rhythm becomes more active developing into sixteenths and sixteenth triplets while the piano stays true to the original theme. A short trill section bridges into a return of the meno mosso material but this time in an agitato character. This is followed by a reprise of the Allegro barbaro section before returning again to the meno mosso material in the original texture and character. This leads into a new section of smorzatos in the bassoon overtop of cluster chords in the piano. Finally, one last return to the first part of the opening material returns to conclude the piece.

description: This is a one-movement work that explores a wide variety of textures from cadenza-like, homorhythmic, and aleatoric. The piece opens with a tam-tam solo and leads into a homorhythmic section for the ensemble. Next, the opening tam-tam solo returns but with a flute melody overtop. Eventually, a virtuosic trill and sixteenth note cadenza in the flute emerges leading into a moderato, march-like homorhythmic section. Next, the oboe begins a more chaotic aleatoric section that is interrupted by percussion solo before returning to more aleatoric material. The common concerto form structure of contrasting solo and tutti sections in either an aleatoric or homorhythmic texture continues for the rest of the piece with the following order of solos: clarinet, cello, violin, and flute.

description: This is a four-movement work that combines elements of chant and renaissance music with avant-garde aesthetics. The first movement “Tranquillo” begins with long notes with varied entrances throughout the ensemble. Eventually, this leads to a homorhythmic section of long notes where the note values get shorter as it progresses until it arrives at quarter notes. This climaxes into a virtuosic trumpet cadenza. The movement ends with another homorhythmic section in the brass overtop of an eighth note accompaniment in the piano. The second movement “Allegro sostenuto” features technical and disjunct lines weaving between the instruments until a solo piano ostinato emerges to end the movement. The third movement “Andante” opens with a solo clarinet long-tones that evolves into a dialogue with the flute overtop of repeated long-tone on the pitch “E” in the piano’s right-hand. This leads into a repeating septuplet and sextuplet sixteenth note section amongst the ensemble. The final movement “Largo” begins with a bassoon solo with other instruments joining in on long tones as it progresses. Eventually, the oboe takes over with a repeated note motif over the long tones to end the piece.

description: This is a one-movement work that combines elements of early music and chant with aesthetics of avant-garde. The first section “Mesto” opens with slow and dissonant double stops in the cello that become consonant in a chant-like manner. This then repeats with the violin. This motif then is repeated by the winds with a disjunct melody in the violin with the cello joining in countermelody eventually. The next section “Senza metro” features a repeated note motif that is contrasted by members of the ensemble singing “kyrie elision” on mono-pitch chant. At the end of the section a harpsichord cadenza appears out of the silence. As it progresses the flute emerges with a stepwise melody that leads to another repeated note motif that is dissonant traded around the ensemble until a flute melody emerges. This is the echoed in the winds until they come together in a tutti scalar motif overtop of arpeggiated sixteenths in the strings leading into the final section “Largo ed un poco piano.” This is a neobaroque character with a clear melody and countermelody overtop of a figured bass accompaniment in the harpsichord and bassoon which is interrupted by a single hit of the tam-tam that slowly fades away. This is the only note the tam-tam plays in the entire piece.

description: This is a one-movement work in an ABA form. The first section “Largo” opens with a slow harp introduction in an arpeggiated texture that begins slow and speeds up as it progresses. Then the oboe enters with a repeated note motif on the pitch “E”, which the bassoon echoes on the pitch “D” while the oboe changes to the pitch “F”. This section continues changing pitches going between consonant and dissonant intervals until arriving at chords in the piano to initiate a new rhythmic motif based on sextuplet sixteenth notes. This leads into a more melodic triplet melody in the bassoon with accompaniment figures in the oboe and piano as an interlude before returning to the harp introduction again. This leads into the repeated note motif with the roles flipped in the oboe and bassoon. The second section “Allegro” is a trading sixteenth note texture between the oboe and bassoon over top of a rhythmic piano accompaniment. This eventually aligns and becomes a full melody with the harp providing countermelody and accompaniment role. This leads into the final section “Andantino” bringing back the opening harp introduction and repeated note motif again.

description: This is a short one-movement work that based on the Ukrainian folk song Oy Chorna (Oh, black). It was written for the Fifteen-Minutes-of-Fame project that is aimed at giving living composers an opportunity to present themselves in short one-minute pieces with a different topic for each concert. This concert was centered around showcasing folk music from different countries. In this piece the folk melody repeats constantly throughout the ensemble while changing the texture surrounding it. It opens in a declamatory manner with just the statement alone. Then a bass line in the bassoon and offbeat ostinato in the horn are added under the melody in the clarinet. Then the bassoon and horn get the melody overtop of a weaving around sixteenth passage in the clarinet leading to a tutti statement of the melody. The final section features the melody in the clarinet with counter melody in the bassoon and horn.

description: This is a three-movement work that explores the idea of one pitch benign expanded upon slowly to evolve into a new section. The first movement “Parlando rubato” begins with a flute solo on a repeated note motif on the pitch “D” that slowly expands lower and returns back to the pitch “D”. The clarinet then joins in rhythmic unison a fifth lower that quickly develops into its own independent line. This continues expanding in both parts until they arrive together again, which the horn enters with their own independent line. This process continues leading to the bassoon entering with an independent line and the oboe entering in unison with all of the instruments interacting together now. The second movement “Scherzando” is a quirky rhythmic and dance-like character with the emphasis changing between beat 3 and 1 based on the placement of accents in the parts. The final movement “Lento” opens with long tones in the clarinet, bassoon and horn with a melody in the flute and countermelody in the oboe. This leads to a repeated note motif that is traded around the ensemble overtop of long tones.

description: This is a one-movement work that explores concepts of sonorism and minimalism through the small development of textures and motifs. The piece begins with long notes alternating through the winds with the entrance marked by an accented sixteenth note in the piano that climaxes to a tutti accented sixteenth note. The next section features one measure phrase of technical quintuplet figures throughout the ensemble arriving at a tutti sixteenth note. Then elements of the two previous sections are combined by having a sixteenth note quintuplets and septuplets in the piano with longer notes in the winds in a scalar motion. This develops in the winds overtime with the note values getting shorter and the line becoming more disjunct leading to a climax of a tutti quarter note in the winds. This then winds down by lengthening the note values and becoming more scalar to end the piece.

description: This is a short three-movement suite that showcases the short articulation, lyrical, and technical capabilities of double reeds. The first movement “Allegro vivace” is an energetic staccato movement consisting mainly of repeated eighth notes. This opens with dissonant repeated eighth notes a semitone apart in the oboes, which the bassoon enters with melodic content. Then a more scalar phrase leading into a contrasting section in a fugal texture before returning to the opening material again but with the melodic content in the first oboe. The second movement “Andante” is a slow contrapuntal texture with whole notes and half notes in the oboes combined with a scalar motif of quarter and half notes in the bassoon. The final movement “Con moto” is a moderate tempo with a weaving texture. The oboes trade sixteenth notes often at unexpected times not in a particular pattern overtop of an eighth note accompaniment in the bassoon.

description: This is a two-movement work that combines aspects of neoclassical such as motifs with contemporary language. The first movement “Largo” is very similar to the “Largo” section in October. The second movement “Allegro giusto con energico'' has an unusual form of ABCDAE. The A section has a sixteenth and eighth note melody that are ornamented in a lively character that utilizes contemporary harmonic language. The B section is a “meno mosso” in a more improvisatory manner with cadenza-like moments. This leads to a short C section with a slow melody played in harmony over a drone-like accompaniment in the piano before a virtuosic D section that is a trading sixteenth section before returning to the opening dance-like section. Then a contrasting “Largo” E section in a drone-like manner appears unexpectedly to end the piece.

premiere: March 3rd, 2004 in Kyiv by Bogdana Stelmashenko (fl), N. Vishtak (ob), Yuri Konrad (bsn)
description: This is a three-movement work inspired by medieval and renaissance music combined with elements of modernism. The first movement “Praeludium” begins with each instrument playing their own line in a cantus-firmus style in staggered entrance that develops into a homorhythmic texture. Eventually, the oboe gets a more soloistic role playing a motif of repeated notes on the pitch “A” combined with fragmented arpeggios that develops into a quasi-cadenza like moment. This returns to a brief section of homorhythmic texture before the flute plays quick flourishes of runs overtop of long tones in the oboe and bassoon. The second movement “Intermedius” begins with a flute solo featuring the repetition of a long note tied to triplets with a grace note motif. Eventually, the bassoon takes this motif over playing it solo. As the bassoon is playing this figure the oboe enters with a virtuosic counterpoint. This eventually leads to a section where all three instruments are in dialogue playing a variation of this virtuosic line. Finally, a section of staggered entry of repeated articulated arpeggios occurs before a grand pause, which takes us back to the original motif to end the movement. The final movement “Cantus” a cantus-firmus line that is displaced through large interval jumps transformed into different characters through three main sections. First, a 5:4 sixteenth note motif that gets traded around the ensemble. Then an articulated repeated note arpeggio that gets traded around the ensemble. Finally, thirty-second notes in descending scalar passage played in unison rhythm concludes the work by gradually becoming a slower rhythmic value over time.

description: This is a three-movement concerto that combines a variety of influences and styles throughout. The premiere of the work received rave reviews from Ukrainian musicologists. The work was described by Mariya Zagaykevych as “discovering the enormous expressive opportunities of the bassoon by revealing moments of expressive meditations, pointed dramatic outbursts, and sincere lyricism.” Sofiya Hrytsa described it as “music that does not shock but impresses all that music can be in the highest spiritual and aesthetic level of perfection with the foremost respect to the listener.” (Bila, 231) The first movement “Sinfonia” is structured with contrasting sections connected together through cadenzas. It opens with the soloist playing a long tone on the pitch “A” that dynamically swells. This pitch is thematically important as it reoccurs throughout the Concerto. With each progressive statement the phrase expands creating a full musical line. The next section “Allegretto” has an intense and insistent character through accented eighth notes and technical articulated sixteenth passages often in a sequential or scalar motion. This section is reminiscent in style of the Jolivet Bassoon Concerto. The orchestra first responds with sequential motifs or direct quotes from the main theme. The next section “Meno mosso” features a low C drone with a quasi-improvisatory line in the bassoon that develops back into an orchestral interlude of the Allegretto material, which leads to a bassoon cadenza in a quasi-improvisatory style. This cadenza is more lyrical in nature and features large interval jumps. The next section shifts characters completely to a neoclassical line in the accompaniment involving a quarter note melody with trills overtop of chords reminiscent of the Classical Era. However, this is disturbed by the presence of polytonality with the music entering in a different key a semitone above with a melody that weaves around trying to find the tonality. This leads into another bassoon cadenza overtop of a C drone. Next, an animato section occurs that combines elements from earlier. The accompaniment has quarter notes, chords, and arpeggiated sixteenths, while the bassoon has aggressive accented fragments that develop into material similar to the allegretto. This develops into the bassoon developing the sixteenth note motif in the orchestra in a virtuosic display. Eventually, a variation of the allegretto material returns with larger intervals and longer lines of sixteenths. Another cadenza occurs to connect into the final allegretto section. The next movement “Aria” opens with an orchestral introduction of whole note chords in an impressionist color and tonality. The bassoon then presents a vocal-like theme alone in a cantabile and legato style. The orchestra plays accompaniment figures as the melody develops throughout the rest of the movement. Eventually, the movement concludes with a large virtuosic cadenza of fast arpeggios requiring double-tonguing from the bassoonist and multiphonics. The final movement “Burlesque” opens with tremolo chords in the strings to create an ominous atmosphere before presenting a theme similar to the theme in the first movement’s allegretto. It begins with three accented repeated notes and includes large intervals but outlining slightly different harmonies. The bassoon responds with this melody before presenting a completely new theme centered around two motifs: 1) eighth followed by two sixteenths and 2) three repeated eighth notes followed by a different eighth note slurred a descending semitone into three more repeated eighth notes. This develops into a fragmented section of two slurred eighth notes in a semitone motion that gets displaced by an octave later on. This leads into a more rhythmically dissonant section where the bassoon has a melody in the lowest octave that weaves around using quarter and eighth note triplets, while the accompaniment has a sixteenth note ostinato. The bassoon ends up joining in on the sixteenths before a return to the original motifs. This leads into a final cadenza combining elements from throughout the concerto such as large intervals, sequential sixteenths, and a lyrical descending eighth note line. An andante section follows utilizing the earlier motif but in a different and more cantabile character in a fugal texture with the orchestra. This leads to an accelerando that brings back the opening bassoon solo material to conclude the work.

This is a one-movement work in ternary form in a neoclassical style intended to provide more repertoire for young performers. The A section is an “allegro” in an energetic and dance-like character. The bassoon has a melodic line featuring staccato eighth notes and slurred sixteenths in the tenor register overtop of accompaniment figures of a quarter note chords and offbeat eighth note chords. The B section “moderato” features a lyrical line of slurred eighth notes that are either stepwise or arpeggiated. The orchestra has half note chords in the bass line combined with a motif of an eighth note rest followed by three staccato eighth notes. The return of the A section brings some slight variations that lead into a final “piu mosso” that is virtuosic in character consisting of long lines of slurred sixteenths in a stepwise or arpeggiated manner.

key: I (E minor), II (A minor), III (C major), IV (E minor), V (C major), VI (C major, E minor)
description: This is a six-movement suite that has alternating movements between a prelude and a fugue resulting in three sets of preludes and fugues. This work is in a neoclassical style following the rules and principles of prelude and fugues established in the Classical Era. A performer could easily perform a selection of either 2 or 4 movements rather than the whole suite, if desired. The first movement “Prelude I” is marked “Andante” and is polyphonic with a melody in the flute, countermelody in the oboe and a bass line in the bassoon for the first section. Then the bassoon presents a new melody while the flute has an ostinato slurred sixteenth note line. Eventually, the flute takes over the melody which is embellished arriving at three measures of homorhythmic chords. The next movement “Fugue I” has a theme of quarter and eighth notes that begins in the bassoon followed by the oboe and flute. “Prelude II” consists of a beat of slurred sixteenths that trade between the flute and oboe over top of long tones and bass line figures in the bassoon. Eventually, the sixteenths align together moving in parallel sixths. Afterwards, the sixteenths trade between the oboe and bassoon, while the flute has a melody that leads back to the opening material to conclude the movement. “Fugue II” has a five-measure introduction of tied whole notes that enter independently throughout the ensemble with four quarter notes in the bassoon leading into the first statement of the theme by the oboe. This theme consists of eighth, quarter and half notes tied to a quarter. The final “Prelude III” opens with a homorhythmic section in a chorale style. The rest of the movement mainly consists of long tones in two of the voices and a melody that leads into a final homorhythmic section. The final “Fugue III” opens with a fourteen measure homorhythm introduction before beginning the theme in the oboe overtop of a bass line in the bassoon. This theme consists of eighth notes with eighth rest inserted throughout.

description: This is a short one movement work in ternary form that highlights the comedic side of the bassoon. The A section features staccato eighth note and sixteenth notes that is contrasted with moments of either accented or tenuto quarter notes. The B section has a more vocal-like melody in bassoon 1, slurred arpeggiated sixteenth notes in bassoons 2-3, and a bass line in bassoon 4. The first 8 measures of the A section returns leading to a fermata measure of silence before a two-measure coda to conclude the piece.

key: D major, G minor, C major
description: This is a one-movement work that utilizes long melodic lines and lush harmonics from romanticism with a virtuosic cadenza. It opens with an “Allegro” section that has a repeated triplet eighth note accompaniment in the orchestra while the bassoon presents a dolce melody. This continues to develop until a small bassoon cadenza that consists of eighth notes leading to a high B and then descends to a low D. The next section begins with fragmented staccato eighth notes that become a full melody in a similar character to the opening. Next, a large and virtuosic bassoon cadenza occurs featuring large intervals and a sequence of arpeggiated sextuplets. The cadenza concludes with a trill on a long tone leading to the opening section returning. However, this time it flirts with tonality going between C major and C minor before returning to the original D major to conclude the work.

This is a short one-movement work in an energetic character. It opens with a repeated note motif consisting of a pattern of eighth and sixteenth notes. This rhythmic motif expands to become a more melodic line. Eventually, 7/8 measures are thrown in to throw off the patterns and rhythmic feel that had been established. This leads into a virtuosic passage of sixteenths in various articulations in a sequential motion that climaxes to the opening motif on the bassoon’s high C. This winds down into a “moderato” section that utilizes material from the alternating 6/8 and 7/8 material. The piece concludes with a tempo primo that includes an arpeggiated sixteenth note passage to a high E followed by a two-measure reprise of the rhythmic motif descending to a low Bb.

description: This is a one-movement work that combines elements of folk song, dance and virtuosity together into one dynamic work. The first section is an “Andante” open with solo bassoon presenting a lyrical melody of eighth, quarter and tied half notes. As the orchestra enters with long tone chords the bassoon melody develops to become more active with more eighth notes filling in the long notes. The next section “Vivace” presents a similar melody with some sixteenths and grace notes added in overtop of the orchestra’s accompaniment eighth note chords often on the downbeats. As it progresses the accompaniment becomes more active and the bassoon melody changes articulation to staccato and accents to intensify. This leads into the next section which features a sixteenth note ostinato in the orchestra with a more disjunct line in the bassoon consisting of two motifs: 1) a sixteenth leading to an eighth note followed by a rest or 2) three repeated sixteenths and a sixteenth rest. Eventually, the motif develops into a full sequential phrase, which involves all four sixteenths leading to an eighth note now. This leads to a more virtuosic section of a passage of slurred sixteenths through the whole range of the bassoon. Next, a “Pesante” section occurs that is an ornamented melody in the bassoon overtop accompaniment figures in the orchestra. To conclude the piece is a short “Andante” section that brings elements of the opening in the bassoon overtop of a drone in the orchestra that leads to a virtuosic arpeggiated triplet passage to a high F (or Db) to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work structured on alternating sections that are inspired by either folk songs or dances. The opening section is an “Andante sostenuto, rubato” that has a vocal-like line based on sixteenths or eighths leading to a longer note centered around A minor. Next, an “Allegretto” section with an alternating 3/8 and 5/8 measures creating a 3+2+3 pattern of eighth notes with the first two notes of the three-grouping slurred creates an energetic dance character. Then the opening section returns now with two voice part writing with the original melody in downwards stems and a countermelody responding in upwards stems. Then a “Allegro marcatissimo” section begins with quarter notes that are jumping between different octaves on the pitch “Bb”. This leads into a slurred sixteenth leading to a eighth note passage that is followed by a syncopated dance-like section achieved through ties over bar lines. This develops into larger interval jumps and the sequence progresses to a high Eb long tone before a descending line of eighth notes to half notes on the pitch “G” to conclude this fiery section. Next an “Un poco meno mosso” section in an espressivo character presents a cantabile vocal-like line in an alternating 2/4 and 3/4 metre pattern. A return to the “Allegro marcatissimo” occurs this time leading to a multiphonic fermata note. A final phrase of the dance-like motif occurs to end the work.

key: I (D major), II (D minor), III (G major) IV (G major), V (E♭ major)
description: This is a five-movement suite in a neoclassical style combining polyphonic and homorhythmic textures. The first movement “Allegretto” is energetic and rhythmic with two main sections. The first section has a bass line in the bassoon and a melody of eighth notes, quarter notes and tied notes in the oboes. This progresses into becoming syncopated with the use of rests inserted. The second section consists of homorhythmic syncopated eighth notes. The next movement “Allegro” opens with a staccato quarter note with a rest on the second beat accompaniment in the oboes underneath a melody in the bassoon. This develops into a homorhythmic line of quarter notes to lead into the second section. It consists of a bass line in the bassoon with a motif consisting of quarter note and three eighth notes in the oboe that develops and variates. This is contrasted with homorhythmic moments of quarter notes or various groupings of eighth notes with an eighth rest. A return to the opening material occurs with the melody in the first oboe this time. This leads into a final homorhythmic accented quarter note section into a sforzando piano on the pitch “C” crescending into three accented eighth notes in an upper neighbour motion. The third movement “Moderato” consists of two main sections. First, long tones combined with a constant stream of eighth notes passed around the ensemble. Second, homorhythmic half notes that alternated between on the beat and time over the bar line leading to two dotted quarter notes to distort the metrical feel of 3/4. This develops back into the eighth note material from earlier. The following movement “Moderato con moto” is mostly homorhythmic, consisting of quarter and half notes with the occasional moments of melody and accompaniment texture. The final movement “Allegretto” consists of sections that begin more homorhythmic and develop into more polyphonic writing with a main motif introduced for each section such as an ascending scalar line of dotted eighth and sixteenth note.

This work consists of four short movements each in a contrasting character to compile a suite utilizing a neoclassical approach to form and phrase structure combined with contemporary harmonic language. The first movement “Melody” is in a moderato tempo. It opens with a slow melody consisting of dotted half and quarter notes in the bassoon overtop of a tremolo in the piano, which evolves in fragmented interjections. The flute initially enters as a countermelody that has moments of unison with the bassoon. This leads to a piu mosso section where the flute and bassoon are trading off, first eighths and then groups of two sixteenths overtop of arpeggiated quintuplets in the piano. The movement continues with the alternating between sections of melody and trading off texture developing into quicker note values and thicker textures. The next movement “Waltz” has a sort of unsettled character as it the stereotypical roles of the waltz are manipulated. The flute plays a melodic line, but it is syncopated with ties combined with flourishes of weaving sixteenths disrupting the natural flow expected. The bassoon provides stability by playing an accompaniment role of dotted quarter notes on the second beat. However, this is thrown off by the piano accompaniment, which starts on the second eighth note of the bar each time. This creates a metrical ambiguity allowing for an unbalanced waltz character to occur. The third movement “Sketch” is in a moderato tempo featuring slow arpeggios and long notes in the piano underneath a quarter note melody in the bassoon. Eventually, the flute enters with glissandos before presenting a more active second melody that develops into a unison motif of arpeggiated quarter notes in the ensemble. The “Final” movement is in allegro molto tempo in ternary form. It opens with a cluster chord motif of two quarter notes that jumps over three octaves between the hands in the piano. This motif creates instability in the 3/4 metre for the winds trading eighth note passages. The B section is a meno mosso with similar lines in the winds but the piano now is in dialogue with the winds eventually becoming unison.

description: This is a short one-movement work in ternary form that uses elements of neoclassical structure combined with stylistic influences from jazz. The A section is divided into an ABA form. The first part is a homorhythmic line of straight-feeling eighth notes leading to a syncopated quarter note in clarinets 1-5 overtop of a quarter note bass line in the bassoon. This section is structured with a first and second ending. The next section are eight measure phrases in a homorhythmic texture built on a syncopated ostinato. The first phrase ends with a solo bass line in the bassoon to connect to the next phrase. A one beat sixteenth note lick in the bassoon leads into a reprise of the opening section. The B section comprises three short sections and switches to a quasi-swing feel through dotted eighth and sixteenth note rhythms and slur markings of the off-beat eighth slurred to the main beat eighth note. The first section has a thicker texture often with a solo line in clarinet 1, homorhythmic accompaniment figures often as little fragments in clarinets 2-5, and a bass line in the bassoon. The second section modulates to the dominant key, A major back to the original homorhythmic texture. However, these phrases are more lyrical and use longer note values such as dotted quarter notes for a contrasting character. This leads into a fermata to set up the final section “meno mosso” which is a solo line in clarinet 1 overtop homorhythmic long tones in the rest of the ensemble. A Da capo al fine provides a return to the A section.

This is a short one-movement work in a neoclassical style that takes inspiration from neoclassicism by utilizing the form of an invention and combining it with more modern motifs, aesthetics and tonal language. The work has a fugal-like texture but plays with the rules and expectations of how the voices should interact. It opens in the left hand of the piano with a semitone eighth note motif between D and Eb that is displaced by an octave on the last eighth. However, the flute enters with a different descending four quarter note motif with the intervals of perfect fourth, semitone, and perfect fourth. This leads into the second half of the motif consisting of an eighth rest followed by seven eighth notes. The bassoon enters during the second measure of the flute’s motif with the same motif, except it is rhythmically displaced with an added quarter note rest between each note in the motif. This allows the ending of the flute’s second statement to line up with the end of the bassoon’s first statement. This section continues to develop in this manner with unexpected treatments of the motifs and breaking of the rules in the flute and bassoon. This is combined with the piano individually developing their motif from measures 1-2. This leads into a short development section where the ensemble is together. The winds weave the second half of the motif between one another overtop of a descending line of accented quarter notes in the piano This leads to a meno mosso section expected to lead back to a recapitulation. Instead, the music winds down to conclude the piece without a recapitulation.

key: I (G major), II (G major, G minor), III (C major)
description: This is a four-movement work in a neoclassical style utilizing compositional techniques and harmony from earlier periods. The first movement “Andantino '' is polyphonic featuring an arpeggiated eighth note motif that has an eighth rest inserted often on the downbeat to disrupt the flow. In the recapitulation this returns as articulated sixteenths on each eighth note. This is combined with a melody and countermelody. The second movement “Allegro” opens with a quarter note line beginning in the bassoon with each oboe added successively to each phrase. This leads into the quarter notes being traded amongst the ensemble. This is alternated with “Andantino” sections that take the melodic content from the first section but changes the rhythm to include a combination of eighth and quarter notes in the bassoon with counter melodies in the oboes in a polyphonic texture. Then a return of the trading eighths occurs that develops into a unison ostinato on the pitch “D”. The next section features a bass line ostinato in the bassoon, an arpeggiated accompaniment in the second oboe and a lyrical melody in the first oboe. This section develops to become more polyphonic and equally independent lines as it modulates to g minor. A return to the opening allegro occurs but in reverse entrance order and long tones until a voice joins the motif. Then the andantino section occurs with some small variations leading to a silent bar. Then one last statement of the trading eighths occurs leading into a forte-piano chord under a fermata to conclude the movement. The third movement “Andante” consists of a polyphonic texture with a couple motifs that repeat throughout. There is an eighth note melody line, staccato sixteenth with rests inserted on either repeated notes or arpeggios, and a sixteenth followed by a dotted eighth note in a descending motion. These motifs develop and are combined in different textures throughout. This leads to a homorhythmic sixteenth note passage repeating two notes in a row in an arpeggiated manner to conclude the movement. The final movement “Allegro scherzando” opens with two accented eighth notes followed by an eighth rest motif that the voices weave in and out of the texture. Eventually, this develops into different motifs that relate, for example flipping it to be eighth note rest followed by four sixteenths in a repeated descending third interval. A new motif is introduced around a neighbour tone motion in two variations: 1) two sixteenths and an eighth under a slur 2) three eighth notes in a neighbour motion. This movement alternates between polyphonic and homorhythmic textures.
